title: SensorPerch: Sense Wherever and Whenever it Matters
summary: Existing robotic perception is constrained by sensors that are either robot-mounted or permanently fixed in the environment, locking perception to a limited set of viewpoints. Yet as robots perform increasingly diverse tasks, the most informative viewpoint shifts from one task to the next-often somewhere onboard sensor and static infrastructure can not readily satisfy. To address this gap, we propose SensorPerch, a novel realization of active perception that decouples sensing from both the robot embodiment and the environment by treating sensors as independent physical entities that the robot can autonomously detach and re-attach within the environment. SensorPerch presents one realization of this paradigm: a lightweight, wireless, reconfigurable sensor platform that can perch on diverse surfaces, paired with a viewpoint-selection framework that determines task-optimal sensor placements. Together, these enable robots to construct task-relevant viewpoints on demand, independent of the robot's current position and available fixed infrastructure. We demonstrate the paradigm on two task classes: (i) object-coupled perception, where SensorPerch enables persistent object-state detection beyond the robot's current position, achieving successful event detection even when the robot is not nearby; and (ii) policy-coupled perception, where SensorPerch allows robots to construct diverse, policy-specific viewpoints for various policies, achieving success rates comparable to those obtained using oracle viewpoints.

AI.tldr: SensorPerch enables robots to autonomously detach and re-attach sensors as independent physical entities, constructing task-relevant viewpoints on demand independent of robot position and fixed infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic perception is constrained by sensors that are either robot-mounted or permanently fixed, limiting available viewpoints. As robots perform diverse tasks, the most informative viewpoint shifts, and static sensors cannot readily satisfy these changing needs.
AI.method: SensorPerch consists of (1) a lightweight, wireless, reconfigurable sensor platform that can perch on diverse surfaces, and (2) a viewpoint-selection framework that determines task-optimal sensor placements. This system decouples sensing from both robot embodiment and environment by treating sensors as independent physical entities.
AI.result: Demonstrated on two task classes: (i) object-coupled perception enabling persistent object-state detection beyond the robot's current position, achieving successful event detection even when the robot is not nearby; and (ii) policy-coupled perception allowing construction of diverse, policy-specific viewpoints with success rates comparable to oracle viewpoints.
AI.conclusion: SensorPerch enables robots to construct task-relevant viewpoints on demand, independent of the robot's current position and available fixed infrastructure, demonstrating the potential of decoupling sensing from robot embodiment and environment through autonomous sensor management.

title: Action Map Policy: Learning 3D Closed-loop Manipulation via Pixel Classification
summary: The action space poses a major challenge in robot learning, since it is often high-dimensional, can span long time horizons, and frequently admits multi-modal optimal solutions. A good choice of action representation and loss function can help to address these concerns, but there are often trade offs. We propose Action Map Policy (AMP), which casts 3D closed-loop manipulation policy learning as a classification problem in image space. While classification has been an effective formulation in generative language models, applying it to robot action learning is difficult because naively discretizing high-dimensional continuous actions explodes the token vocabulary. Our key idea is to project 3D actions onto the camera image planes and treat each pixel location as a discrete class, thus controlling dimensionality while retaining multi-modality. This method supports millimeter-level precision for high-dimensional actions without requiring a prohibitively large vocabulary, while preserving fine-grained pixel-wise visual signals. Furthermore, it can predict the entire action chunk in a single forward pass, avoiding complex noise scheduling and iterative denoising while achieving substantially faster inference than diffusion policies. Experiments on various manipulation tasks show that AMP outperforms strong baselines, achieving higher success rates, faster inference, and enhanced spatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: AMP casts 3D closed-loop manipulation policy learning as an image-space classification problem by projecting 3D actions onto camera planes, treating each pixel as a discrete class to enable millimeter-level precision without large vocabularies.
AI.motivation: Robot action spaces are high-dimensional, long-horizon, and multi-modal, making them challenging to learn. While action representation and loss function design can help, naive discretization of continuous actions creates prohibitively large token vocabularies, and existing approaches like diffusion policies require complex noise scheduling and iterative denoising.
AI.method: AMP projects 3D actions onto camera image planes and treats each pixel location as a discrete class. This approach maintains multi-modality while controlling dimensionality, allowing pixel-wise visual signals to be preserved. It predicts entire action chunks in a single forward pass without iterative denoising.
AI.result: AMP outperforms strong baselines across various manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates, faster inference (substantially faster than diffusion policies), and enhanced spatial reasoning. It enables millimeter-level precision for high-dimensional actions without requiring prohibitively large vocabularies.
AI.conclusion: AMP successfully addresses the trade-offs in action representation by enabling precise, high-dimensional action learning through a classification-based approach in image space. The method eliminates the need for complex noise scheduling and iterative denoising while providing significantly faster inference speeds compared to diffusion policies.

title: Learning Roller-Skating Motions of Humanoid Robots Based on Adversarial Motion Priors
comment: 12 pages. Submitted preprint version. Accepted for oral presentation at CLAWAR 2026
summary: Humanoid roller-skating is difficult because the robot must coordinate whole-body balance, rolling contacts, and velocity-dependent posture regulation. This paper presents an adversarial motion prior based reinforcement learning framework for two humanoid roller-skating gaits: Pump Glide skating and Push Glide skating. The two gait datasets are collected independently through motion capture and retargeted to the humanoid robot separately. The retargeted data are then smoothed and resampled into reference motion states for AMP training. The two gaits are learned by independent AMP training pipelines with separate reference datasets, separate policies, and independent reward architectures. Simulation experiments are designed to evaluate gait quality, velocity tracking, turning, and gait-specific reward ablations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an adversarial motion prior (AMP) based reinforcement learning framework for two humanoid roller-skating gaits (Pump Glide and Push Glide), trained with independent policies, reward architectures, and reference datasets derived from motion capture data.
AI.motivation: Humanoid roller-skating is challenging because the robot must coordinate whole-body balance, rolling contacts, and velocity-dependent posture regulation.
AI.method: The researchers collect motion capture data for Pump Glide and Push Glide skating, retarget it to a humanoid robot, smooth and resample it into reference motion states, and train separate AMP training pipelines with independent policies, reward architectures, and reference datasets for each gait.
AI.result: Simulation experiments evaluate gait quality, velocity tracking, turning ability, and perform reward ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables effective learning of humanoid roller-skating gaits by combining motion capture priors with reinforcement learning.

title: D-SafeMPC: Diffusion-Driven Safe Model Predictive Control with Discrete-Time Control Barrier Functions
summary: A key limitation on the use of diffusion models in robotic planning is their inability to inherently enforce safety or dynamical constraints, which often results in physically infeasible or unsafe outputs. Hybrid approaches that employ model predictive control (MPC) to address this problem can be unstable, as poor trajectory initializations from the diffusion model prevent the MPC from converging to a safe and feasible solution. To overcome these challenges, we propose D-SafeMPC, which enhances the interaction between diffusion and control. Our method guides the reverse diffusion process with control barrier functions (CBFs) and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) and employs an iterative-projection scheme where an MPC refines the trajectory at each denoising step. This steers sampling toward safe, goal-directed regions and provides reliable MPC warm starts. In simulations on a Franka manipulator across four scenarios (one static-obstacle and three dynamic-obstacle settings) and in a sim-to-real experiment on a physical Franka robot, D-SafeMPC improves safety, task success rates, and planning efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines. To facilitate reproducibility, our source code and experimental configurations are available in a repository at https://github.com/erdiphd/D-SafeMPC

AI.tldr: D-SafeMPC enhances the interaction between diffusion models and control by guiding the reverse diffusion process with control barrier functions (CBFs) and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs), and employing an iterative-projection scheme where model predictive control (MPC) refines trajectories at each denoising step.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models lack inherent safety and dynamical constraints, often producing physically infeasible outputs. Hybrid MPC approaches can be unstable due to poor trajectory initializations from diffusion models that prevent MPC convergence.
AI.method: The authors propose D-SafeMPC, which (1) guides the reverse diffusion process using CBFs and CLFs, and (2) employs an iterative-projection scheme where MPC refines the trajectory at each denoising step.
AI.result: The method improves safety, task success rates, and planning efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines across four scenarios in simulation (Franka manipulator with static and dynamic obstacles) and in a sim-to-real experiment on a physical Franka robot.
AI.conclusion: By integrating CBFs, CLFs, and iterative MPC refinement into the diffusion process, D-SafeMPC effectively addresses the safety and feasibility challenges in robotic planning, demonstrating significant improvements in both simulation and real-world deployment.

title: 3D Scene Graph Prediction: Generating Hierarchical Models from Partially Observed Environments
comment: Accepted at IROS 2026. Main paper: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Includes a supplementary appendix
summary: Generating realistic 3D indoor scenes is an area of growing interest in computer vision and robotics. Existing methods, often motivated by applications such as interior design, generally focus on object layout generation within a single room. The generation of high-level scene structure, such as room-level layout and traversability, remains underexplored despite its importance for robotics applications. In this paper, we consider the case where a robot has explored part of an environment and needs to predict the unexplored parts to support downstream tasks such as exploration or object search. We propose a top-down framework for synthesizing hierarchical 3D scene graphs, including a room layer -- describing the floor plan and traversability -- and an object layer modeling object layouts within each room. For the room layer, we propose a novel mixed-domain graph diffusion model jointly predicting room categories, floor boundaries, and traversability between rooms. Via corruption and masking, this model supports partial constraints such as incomplete floor plans, avoiding the need for partially observed training data. For the object layer, we integrate an existing mixed discrete-continuous diffusion model for joint prediction of object categories, locations, sizes, and orientations within each room given the floor plan. We compare our method with state-of-the-art occupancy-based and LLM-based floor plan generation methods on a standard benchmark. Compared with an occupancy-based learning baseline, our method generalizes substantially better to out-of-distribution partial floor plans. We also demonstrate our integrated prediction pipeline on real-world scenes from robot-collected data, enabling prediction beyond explored areas.

AI.tldr: A top-down framework for hierarchical 3D scene graph synthesis, combining a room layer (floor plan and traversability via mixed-domain graph diffusion) with an object layer (object layouts via mixed discrete-continuous diffusion), enabling prediction of unexplored parts of indoor environments for robotics applications.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D indoor scene generation methods focus on single-room object layout generation, while high-level scene structure (room-level layout and traversability) remains underexplored despite its critical importance for robotics applications such as exploration and object search. The paper addresses the scenario where a robot has explored part of an environment and needs to predict unexplored regions.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical 3D scene graph synthesis framework with two layers: (1) Room layer using a novel mixed-domain graph diffusion model to jointly predict room categories, floor boundaries, and traversability, supporting partial constraints via corruption and masking; (2) Object layer integrating an existing mixed discrete-continuous diffusion model to jointly predict object categories, locations, sizes, and orientations within each room given the floor plan.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art occupancy-based and LLM-based floor plan generation methods on a standard benchmark, the proposed method generalizes substantially better to out-of-distribution partial floor plans than occupancy-based learning baselines. Demonstrated on real-world scenes from robot-collected data, the pipeline enables prediction beyond explored areas.
AI.conclusion: The integrated top-down prediction pipeline effectively synthesizes hierarchical 3D scene graphs including room-level layout and traversability along with object layouts, providing superior generalization capabilities compared to occupancy-based approaches for predicting unexplored parts of indoor environments.

title: A Single Diffusion-Policy Controller for Multi-Task Block Pushing with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
summary: Diffusion policies have shown promising empirical performance in representing and learning complex maneuvers for robots using behavior cloning (BC). In this paper, we explore training diffusion policies from scratch using reinforcement learning (RL) for multi-task robotic manipulation. Specifically, we aim to train a single diffusion policy for block-pushing tasks with multiple shapes. The proposed framework features a simple policy loss function, which is a reweighted evidence lower bound used in BC-based diffusion policy training and can seamlessly serve as the policy learning module in RL algorithms. To address the exploration challenges arising from the absence of demonstrations, we incorporate reverse curriculum generation and objective-centric representations. Combined with the expressiveness of diffusion policies, our design supports learning of multi-task block-pushing policies in our sparse-reward simulation setting. We further evaluate whether the trained diffusion policy transfers in zero-shot to real-world tasks under varying environmental conditions including goal positions, block shapes, block weights and surface friction, providing evidence that this pipeline can transfer to our real-world block-pushing setup under the tested variations.

AI.tldr: This paper explores training diffusion policies from scratch using reinforcement learning (RL) for multi-task robotic manipulation, specifically block-pushing tasks with multiple shapes. By incorporating reverse curriculum generation and objective-centric representations alongside a reweighted evidence lower bound policy loss, the approach enables effective exploration in sparse-reward environments and achieves zero-shot transfer to real-world block-pushing under varying conditions.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies have demonstrated promising empirical performance in representing and learning complex robot maneuvers using behavior cloning (BC). However, the authors aim to explore training diffusion policies from scratch using reinforcement learning (RL) for multi-task robotic manipulation, moving beyond the BC paradigm.
AI.method: The proposed framework includes: (1) a simple policy loss function based on a reweighted evidence lower bound used in BC-based diffusion policy training; (2) reverse curriculum generation to address exploration challenges in the absence of demonstrations; (3) objective-centric representations; and (4) leveraging the inherent expressiveness of diffusion policies.
AI.result: The design successfully learns multi-task block-pushing policies in a sparse-reward simulation setting. The trained diffusion policy transfers in zero-shot to real-world block-pushing tasks under varying environmental conditions including different goal positions, block shapes, block weights, and surface friction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline demonstrates the feasibility of training diffusion policies from scratch using RL with reverse curriculum generation and objective-centric representations, achieving both effective multi-task learning in simulation and zero-shot transfer to real-world block-pushing under tested environmental variations.

title: Mapping Pamir: Multi-Session Visual-Inertial SLAM and 3D Reconstruction of an Underwater Shipwreck
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures. Accepted to ICRA 2026, Vienna, Austria
summary: This paper presents a framework for multi-session mapping of underwater environments utilizing an affordable action camera. The Visual-Inertial data are augmented by water depth recordings from a dive computer. title: Real-Time Rulebook-Aware Nonlinear MPC for Autonomous Driving with Priority-Biased Tiered Slacks
comment: The manuscript is submitted to the Journal of Control Engineering Practice, A journal of The International Federation of Automatic Control (IFAC)
summary: Autonomous-vehicle motion planners must resolve conflicts among safety, regulation, comfort, and efficiency in real time while exposing those decisions for audit. We present W-SQP, a weighted tiered-slack nonlinear model predictive controller (NMPC) that compiles nine driving-rule families into a four-tier shared-slack nonlinear program solved online with CasADi and IPOPT; the name denotes the weighted quadratic slack penalty, not a sequential-quadratic-programming solver. Strongly separated tier penalties bias residual violations toward lower-priority rules while leaving actuation bounds hard. The controller replans from its executed state at $10$\,Hz and records per-rule residuals on every cycle. A $90$\,ms solver-time limit returns an anytime iterate that is projected through the vehicle dynamics before execution; median and maximum observed wall-clock solve times were $28$ and $104$\,ms. We evaluate W-SQP in closed loop on 150 Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios in Waymax against reactive and proposal-and-select baselines, and introduce a log-independent protocol that separates safety and regulatory compliance from resemblance to the recorded human trajectory. Under this protocol, W-SQP shows no systematic group-level deficit relative to expert replay on the log-independent safety and regulatory rules, with several localized regressions in the hardest, highest-divergence scenarios. The results characterize W-SQP as an auditable, priority-biased, anytime-capable NMPC prototype rather than a hard-real-time or formally safe controller.

AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicle motion planners must resolve conflicts among safety, regulation, comfort, and efficiency in real time while also exposing those decisions for audit.
AI.method: W-SQP compiles nine driving-rule families into a four-tier shared-slack nonlinear program solved online with CasADi and IPOPT using weighted quadratic slack penalties to bias residual violations toward lower-priority rules. The controller replans from executed state at 10Hz with 90ms solver-time limit, recording per-rule residuals on every cycle.

title: Think When It Matters: Conditional VLM Reasoning for Social Navigation with RL Policies
summary: As mobile robots become more integrated into everyday human environments, social robot navigation is becoming essential for ensuring human comfort, safety, and trust. While reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policies provide the fast inference and reactive behavior necessary for real-time deployment, they still lack flexible semantic reasoning capabilities and often fail to generalize to complex social scenarios. Recent approaches have increasingly turned to vision-language models (VLMs) in place of RL policies to improve semantic and social reasoning in robot navigation. Nevertheless, their high computational cost and slow inference remain major barriers to real-time deployment. To overcome these limitations, we introduce HUMA (Hybrid Understanding for Multi-modal social Navigation), a hybrid architecture that dynamically balances the computational efficiency of RL policies with the deep semantic understanding of VLMs. Our approach uses a reactive RL policy to handle low-density, routine navigation tasks, while conditioning it on a post-trained high-level VLM when a human enters sensitive situations, such as the robot's proximity zone. We evaluate HUMA on the Social-MP3D and Social-HM3D benchmarks, where it achieves task success improvements of 20% and 3%, respectively, while significantly reducing personal space violations and human collisions against state-of-the-art baselines. Extensive ablation studies validate each architectural component, and real-world deployment on the Mirokaï mobile robot further demonstrates the practical viability of our approach.

AI.tldr: HUMA introduces a hybrid architecture combining fast reactive RL policies with deep semantic understanding from vision-language models for social robot navigation, achieving 20% task success improvement on Social-MP3D and 3% on Social-HM3D while reducing collisions and space violations.
AI.motivation: RL navigation policies provide fast inference but lack flexible semantic reasoning and generalization; VLMs improve semantic understanding but have high computational cost and slow inference, creating a barrier to real-time deployment in human environments.
AI.method: HUMA dynamically balances computational efficiency and semantic understanding by using a reactive RL policy for routine navigation tasks and conditioning it on a post-trained VLM when humans enter sensitive proximity zones, enabling context-aware decision making without constant VLM inference.
AI.result: Achieves 20% task success improvement on Social-MP3D and 3% on Social-HM3D benchmarks, significantly reduces personal space violations and human collisions against state-of-the-art baselines, validated through ablation studies and real-world deployment on Mirokaï mobile robot.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates practical viability by successfully balancing the fast inference of RL policies with the deep semantic understanding of VLMs, enabling real-time social navigation in complex human environments.

title: Wearing A Coat: Dual-Arm Robot-Assisted Dressing with Differentiable Clothing Simulation
summary: The development of assistive robots for dressing tasks serves to augment human convenience and improve the quality of life for individuals with physical impairments. However, due to the intricate contact interactions between garments and the human limbs during dressing, most robot-assisted dressing algorithms treat clothing as an assembly of discrete segments, thereby struggling to manage the partial worn garments under contact constraints. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel robotic dressing control algorithm that integrates realtime differentiable clothing simulation. The simulation algorithm employs explicit iterative scheme with intentionally introduced higher-order perturbations to enhance computational efficiency while maintaining stability under large time-step conditions. Through simulation, we resolve the garment state under contact constraints, which then enables a multi-phase control strategy for successful coat dressing assistance. To further improve real-time performance, we introduce a constrained local model along with its corresponding optimization solver, permitting high-frequency local compensation for the differentiable simulation based global controller. Finally, we experimentally validate our approach through both simulated and physical dressing scenarios, conclusively demonstrating its feasibility and efficacy

AI.tldr: A novel robotic dressing control algorithm that integrates real-time differentiable clothing simulation with explicit iterative schemes and constrained local models to successfully handle complex garment-limb contact interactions during assisted dressing tasks.
AI.motivation: Assistive robots for dressing tasks improve quality of life for individuals with physical impairments, but current algorithms struggle because they treat clothing as discrete segments and cannot properly manage partial worn garments under contact constraints.
AI.method: The proposed approach integrates real-time differentiable clothing simulation using an explicit iterative scheme with higher-order perturbations for computational efficiency and stability. It resolves garment states under contact constraints and employs a multi-phase control strategy for coat dressing. A constrained local model with an optimization solver enables high-frequency local compensation for the differentiable simulation-based global controller.
AI.result: Experimental validation in both simulated and physical dressing scenarios demonstrates the feasibility and efficacy of the proposed algorithm.
AI.conclusion: The integrated differentiable simulation and multi-phase control strategy successfully addresses the challenge of managing complex garment-limb interactions, proving viable for practical robotic dressing assistance applications.

title: Affordance-Based Manipulation Planning with Text Goals and Sim-to-Real Generalisation via Real-to-Sim Image Conversion
summary: We present a manipulation planning system based on affordance recognition and action effect prediction. The system reasons through possible futures in visual form, and evaluates candidate plans by agreement of predicted outcomes with text-based goals set at run-time, using a multi-modal goal-matching module. Positions of objects named in the goal text are tracked through predictions even when occluded, making it possible to generate action plans even when objects become occluded, or when their initial descriptors cease to identify them in future states. We further expand the system with an image conversion module for translating real-world state images with objects of varied shapes and visual appearances into a consistent visual appearance, to facilitate manipulation planning in a physical robot setup. We evaluate performance of the system's modules in isolation and demonstrate the integrated system's manipulation planning capabilities on a set of challenging tasks in both simulation and on hardware.

AI.tldr: A manipulation planning system based on affordance recognition and action effect prediction that reasons through possible futures, evaluates plans via multi-modal goal-matching, and tracks occluded objects through predictions.
AI.motivation: To enable manipulation planning in scenarios where objects become occluded or their initial descriptors cease to identify them in future states, and to facilitate manipulation planning in physical robot setups by handling varied object shapes and visual appearances.
AI.method: The system combines affordance recognition and action effect prediction, uses a multi-modal goal-matching module to evaluate candidate plans against text-based goals, tracks object positions through predictions even when occluded, and includes an image conversion module to translate real-world state images with varied object appearances into a consistent visual representation.
AI.result: Performance of individual modules was evaluated in isolation, and the integrated system demonstrated manipulation planning capabilities on challenging tasks in both simulation and hardware environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system successfully performs manipulation planning on challenging tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining affordance recognition, action effect prediction, and multi-modal goal matching for robot manipulation.

title: Whole-Body Semantic-to-Actuation Grounding of Elephant-Inspired Soft-Trunk Motion via Lightweight Flow Matching
summary: For close-contact human-robot interaction (HRI), trunk-like continuum manipulators provide a physical channel for diverse whole-body expression, but grounding open-vocabulary responses into such robots is difficult: end-effector motion underspecifies body shape, whereas direct whole-body commands are high-dimensional and hard to keep feasible. We propose a whole-body semantic-to-actuation grounding framework for elephant-inspired soft-trunk HRI based on lightweight flow matching. The framework converts responses from a multimodal large language model into bounded, morphology-aligned intent-intensity tuples, parameterizes tendon-actuation trajectories with compact Catmull-Rom spline controls, and uses a rectified-flow generator to sample feasible whole-body trunk motions. Experiments show that the proposed framework improves held-out grounding correctness from 25.0% to 77.2% over a raw-response dense-regression baseline. Compared with a denoising-diffusion baseline, it improves correctness from 71.9% to 77.2% and reduces inference time from 7.86 ms to 4.87 ms while preserving motion diversity. A 100-participant physical HRI study further shows that adding the generated soft-trunk motion channel increases the positive overall-satisfaction rating from 46% to 82% over the audiovisual-only baseline.

AI.tldr: A whole-body semantic-to-actuation grounding framework for elephant-inspired soft-trunk HRI using lightweight flow matching, which converts multimodal LLM responses into morphology-aligned intent-intensity tuples, parameterizes tendon-actuation with Catmull-Rom splines, and uses rectified-flow generators to produce feasible whole-body trunk motions, improving grounding correctness from 25.0% to 77.2% and increasing positive satisfaction ratings from 46% to 82% in physical HRI studies.
AI.motivation: Close-contact HRI with trunk-like continuum manipulators enables diverse whole-body expression but presents two key challenges: (1) end-effector motion alone is insufficient to fully specify body shape, and (2) direct whole-body commands are high-dimensional and difficult to maintain feasibility. The goal is to ground open-vocabulary responses from multimodal LLMs into physically feasible whole-body motions for elephant-inspired soft-trunk robots.
AI.method: The proposed framework employs three key components: (1) converts multimodal LLM responses into bounded, morphology-aligned intent-intensity tuples; (2) parameterizes tendon-actuation trajectories using compact Catmull-Rom spline controls; and (3) utilizes a rectified-flow generator to sample feasible whole-body trunk motions. The approach is built on lightweight flow matching, which enables efficient sampling of physically valid trajectories.
AI.result: The framework achieved significant improvements: (1) held-out grounding correctness increased from 25.0% to 77.2% over a raw-response dense-regression baseline; (2) compared to a denoising-diffusion baseline, correctness improved from 71.9% to 77.2% while reducing inference time from 7.86 ms to 4.87 ms; (3) a physical HRI study with 100 participants showed positive overall-satisfaction ratings increasing from 46% to 82% over an audiovisual-only baseline, demonstrating that adding the soft-trunk motion channel significantly enhances user experience.
AI.conclusion: The lightweight flow matching framework successfully addresses the challenge of grounding open-vocabulary responses into physically feasible whole-body motions for elephant-inspired soft-trunk HRI. By converting semantic responses into morphology-aligned intent-intensity tuples and using compact spline controls with rectified-flow generation, the approach achieves high grounding correctness (77.2%), faster inference (4.87 ms), and significantly improved user satisfaction (82% positive ratings). This demonstrates the practical viability of integrating continuous trunk manipulators into close-contact human-robot interaction systems.

title: SegDiff: Segmented Trajectory Diffusion for Consistent and Adaptive Robot Manipulation
summary: Imitation learning enables robots to acquire manipulation skills from demonstrations by mapping observations to actions. Existing approaches predict either short-horizon continuous action sequences or discrete keyposes. However, continuous prediction methods suffer from compounding errors due to short prediction horizons and struggle with multi-modal action distributions, whereas keypose-based methods necessitate an external planner, constraining real-time applicability. To address these challenges, we introduce SegDiff, a closed-loop visuomotor policy that integrates the strengths of both paradigms. SegDiff decomposes demonstrations into motion segments between keyposes and learns to predict the continuous trajectory from the current state to the next keypose, enabling long-horizon prediction with real-time refinement. Furthermore, we leverage the capability of diffusion models and DDIM inversion to propose a Dynamic Temporal Ensembling mechanism, which allows the policy to efficiently respond to dynamic environments and mitigate discontinuities caused by inconsistent multi-modal sampling. SegDiff demonstrates significant performance gains over existing approaches across various simulated and real-world scenarios, indicating its strong ability to reason over extended temporal dependencies while maintaining real-time adaptability and control stability.

AI.tldr: SegDiff is a closed-loop visuomotor policy that integrates continuous trajectory prediction with keypose-based methods using diffusion models and DDIM inversion to enable long-horizon manipulation skills with real-time adaptability.
AI.motivation: Existing imitation learning approaches face two fundamental trade-offs: continuous prediction methods suffer from compounding errors due to short horizons and struggle with multi-modal action distributions, while keypose-based methods require external planners that limit real-time applicability. The authors seek to combine the strengths of both paradigms.
AI.method: SegDiff decomposes demonstrations into motion segments between keyposes and learns to predict continuous trajectories from the current state to the next keypose. It leverages diffusion models and DDIM inversion to implement a Dynamic Temporal Ensembling mechanism that enables efficient response to dynamic environments and mitigates discontinuities from inconsistent multi-modal sampling.
AI.result: SegDiff demonstrates significant performance gains over existing approaches across various simulated and real-world scenarios, showing strong ability to reason over extended temporal dependencies while maintaining real-time adaptability and control stability.
AI.conclusion: SegDiff successfully integrates the advantages of continuous prediction and keypose-based methods, effectively addressing the limitations of both approaches and proving effective for long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring real-time performance.

title: Learning to Navigate Efficiently with Only 0.58M Trainable Parameters
summary: Recent progress in visual navigation has largely been driven by scale: end-to-end policies with hundreds of millions of parameters trained on billions of frames or large-scale simulated data. We ask how much of this scale a single task family actually requires, and what structure can substitute for it. We propose a decomposed navigation model in which operations with known closed-form structure, such as projective geometry, occupancy, and coordinate transforms, are computed analytically and serve as interfaces between three small learned modules: an egress predictor that grounds the episode goal as a local subgoal in the current view, a navigation predictor that estimates a goal-conditioned posterior over where trajectories travel, and an endpoint-pinned residual diffusion generator that samples trajectory shapes from this posterior. The system trains only 0.58M out of a total of 22.7M parameters, on 44k frames in under one GPU-hour, yet approaches the performance of state-of-the-art models on navigation tasks across 6060 point-goal episodes and 60 environments, while having 233x fewer trainable parameters, the lowest collision rate among all evaluated methods, and 50 Hz inference speed. The decomposition further transfers to no-goal exploration by retraining only the 123k-parameter egress head, and its failure modes under sensor corruption are transparent and analytically correctable.

AI.tldr: A decomposed navigation model using analytical geometric operations instead of massive neural networks, achieving SOTA performance with 233x fewer parameters, 50 Hz speed, and lowest collision rate.
AI.motivation: Recent visual navigation progress relies heavily on scale (billions of frames, hundreds of millions of parameters). The authors question how much scale is actually needed and what structured alternatives can substitute for massive neural networks.
AI.method: Proposes a decomposed navigation model with three small learned modules (egress predictor, navigation predictor, endpoint-pinned residual diffusion generator) connected by analytically computed operations (projective geometry, occupancy, coordinate transforms). Only 0.58M of 22.7M parameters are trainable.
AI.result: Trains on 44k frames in under 1 GPU hour. Achieves comparable SOTA performance on 6060 point-goal episodes across 60 environments with 233x fewer trainable parameters, lowest collision rate, and 50 Hz inference speed. Transfers to no-goal exploration by retraining only the 123k-parameter egress head.
AI.conclusion: Decomposed navigation with analytical structure can achieve state-of-the-art performance with dramatically fewer resources, better safety (lower collision rate), and transparent failure modes that are analytically correctable under sensor corruption.

title: GraspGraphNet: Graph-Structured Multi-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
summary: Dexterous grasp generation across robot hands is challenging because hands differ in kinematic topology, actuation dimensions, and native command spaces. We introduce GraspGraphNet, a topology-aware grasp generation framework that represents each hand as a URDF-derived kinematic graph and directly generates executable palm poses and joint configurations. GraspGraphNet combines hierarchical object surface encoding, differentiable forward kinematics, and dynamic world-edge message passing to model evolving robot-object interactions. It applies conditional flow matching directly in executable palm-pose and joint-state space, avoiding post-processing optimization, inverse kinematics, and retargeting. Using a shared model trained on Barrett Hand, Allegro Hand, and Shadow Hand, GraspGraphNet achieves an average success rate of 83.48% with 40ms inference time per grasp on a 40-object benchmark. Without retraining, the same model achieves 72.70% success on controlled finger-removal variants, demonstrating robustness to hand-topology variations. These results suggest that graph-structured hand representations can effectively support dexterous grasp generation across robot hands with different kinematic structures. Project: https://lysees.github.io/graspgraphnet-page

AI.tldr: A topology-aware grasp generation framework called GraspGraphNet that uses graph representations of robot hands to generate executable grasps across different hand topologies.
AI.motivation: Dexterous grasp generation across robot hands is challenging because hands differ in kinematic topology, actuation dimensions, and native command spaces.
AI.method: GraspGraphNet represents hands as URDF-derived kinematic graphs, combines hierarchical object surface encoding, differentiable forward kinematics, and dynamic world-edge message passing, and applies conditional flow matching directly in palm-pose and joint-state space, avoiding post-processing optimization, inverse kinematics, and retargeting.
AI.result: Achieves 83.48% average success rate with 40ms inference time per grasp on a 40-object benchmark, and 72.70% success on controlled finger-removal variants without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured hand representations can effectively support dexterous grasp generation across robot hands with different kinematic structures.

title: PAKE: Learning Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation with Partial Kinematic Embeddings
summary: Loco-manipulation has recently shown promising capabilities; however, achieving high-precision control, managing the high-dimensional action space induced by many degrees of freedom (DoFs), and fully exploiting the inherent redundancy of whole-body systems remain challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel whole-body control framework that effectively addresses these challenges by decomposing the complex loco-manipulation problem into partial reference motion generation and low-level imitation control. We introduce a new Kinematic Normalizing Flow (KNF) model, trained on a large-scale kinematic dataset, that generates diverse yet feasible partial reference motions. A high-level controller is then trained to navigate the KNF's latent space to exploit redundant solutions, while a low-level controller ensures physically feasible and accurate motion execution. We validate our approach on the quadrupedal robot equipped with a six-DoF robotic arm. In simulation, experimental results show that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of tracking accuracy and feasible workspace coverage. For hardware deployment, we evaluate the system over 24 episodes across 8 different mobile loco-manipulation tasks. The system achieves end-effector pose-tracking errors of 4.5 cm and 0.14 rad, while maintaining accurate locomotion tracking with linear and angular velocity errors of 0.1 m/s and 0.01 rad/s, respectively, outperforming competitive baselines. Our method represents a practical and powerful solution for accurate and generalized whole-body loco-manipulation in high-DoF robotic systems, with promising potential for diverse downstream robotic tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a whole-body control framework for loco-manipulation that decomposes the problem into partial reference motion generation (via a Kinematic Normalizing Flow model) and low-level imitation control. The approach achieves high-precision control on a quadrupedal robot with a 6-DoF arm, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both simulation and real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Locomanipulation faces challenges in achieving high-precision control, managing high-dimensional action spaces from many degrees of freedom, and fully exploiting the inherent redundancy of whole-body systems.
AI.method: The approach decomposes the loco-manipulation problem into: (1) A Kinematic Normalizing Flow (KNF) model trained on large-scale kinematic data to generate diverse yet feasible partial reference motions, with a high-level controller navigating the KNF's latent space to exploit redundant solutions; (2) A low-level controller ensuring physically feasible and accurate motion execution.
AI.result: In simulation, the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in tracking accuracy and feasible workspace coverage. For hardware deployment across 8 different mobile loco-manipulation tasks (24 episodes), the system achieves end-effector pose-tracking errors of 4.5 cm and 0.14 rad, while maintaining locomotion tracking with linear and angular velocity errors of 0.1 m/s and 0.01 rad/s, outperforming competitive baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method represents a practical and powerful solution for accurate and generalized whole-body loco-manipulation in high-DoF robotic systems, with promising potential for diverse downstream robotic tasks.

title: Desc++: Efficient Descriptor Enhancement for Data Association in Existing Visual SLAM Systems
summary: Reliable visual data association is fundamental to visual SLAM (V-SLAM), as it directly determines the quality of the camera pose estimation and map consistency. However, the handcrafted descriptors used by most mature real-time systems degrade under illumination and viewpoint changes, while learning-based front-ends that address this weakness typically require replacing the extraction-and-matching pipeline and introduce substantial computational overhead. Descriptor enhancement offers a compromise by refining existing descriptors within their original format, yet current methods rely on simplified attention mechanisms whose limited contextual modeling constrains the achievable matching quality. To resolve this trade-off between contextual expressiveness and efficiency, we propose Desc++, a lightweight enhancement module that jointly encodes descriptor representations and keypoint geometry and aggregates spatial context through a hybrid architecture that combines order-agnostic global attention with geometry-aware sequential modeling in linear time. The enhanced descriptors retain their original dimensionality and matching interface, enabling integration into deployed V-SLAM systems without modifying the pipeline. Experiments across descriptor matching, correspondence analysis, and system-level benchmarks with four different V-SLAM systems demonstrate that Desc++ improves matching accuracy over the state-of-the-art enhancement method, translates these gains into more accurate and stable trajectory estimation, and achieves a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency for practical integration into existing real-time V-SLAM pipelines.

AI.tldr: Desc++ is a lightweight descriptor enhancement module for V-SLAM that combines order-agnostic global attention with geometry-aware sequential modeling to improve matching accuracy and trajectory estimation while maintaining linear computational complexity.
AI.motivation: Handcrafted descriptors degrade under illumination and viewpoint changes in V-SLAM, while learning-based front-ends require pipeline replacement and substantial computational overhead. Existing descriptor enhancement methods rely on simplified attention mechanisms with limited contextual modeling, creating a trade-off between expressiveness and efficiency.
AI.method: Desc++ jointly encodes descriptor representations and keypoint geometry, aggregating spatial context through a hybrid architecture combining order-agnostic global attention with geometry-aware sequential modeling in linear time. The enhanced descriptors retain original dimensionality and matching interface, enabling integration without pipeline modification.
AI.result: Desc++ improves matching accuracy over state-of-the-art enhancement methods and translates to more accurate and stable trajectory estimation across four different V-SLAM systems. It achieves a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency, maintaining compatibility with existing real-time V-SLAM pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Desc++ resolves the trade-off between contextual expressiveness and efficiency in descriptor enhancement for V-SLAM. The proposed lightweight module successfully integrates into deployed systems, providing practical improvements in visual data association quality without requiring pipeline changes or excessive computational resources.

title: VIA: Visual Interface Agent for Robot Control
summary: Robot manipulation is a complex task that requires visual understanding, physical reasoning, planning, and closed-loop control. General-purpose foundation models (FMs) have grown remarkably capable of some of these, especially vision and reasoning. To leverage this for generalist robot policies, current methods typically involve converting existing FMs into vision-language-action (VLA) models by fine-tuning on robot data to output low-level actions. However, VLAs are often orders of magnitude smaller than frontier FMs given the limited data and compute available for fine-tuning, which in turn limits their general capability. Inspired by the growing ability of FMs to operate software through visual interfaces, we ask whether that same competence suffices to control a robot. We present VIA (Visual Interface Agent for robot control), a framework that recasts robot control as an agentic task: an off-the-shelf FM-powered agent drives a manipulator through a browser-based 3D interface by taking screenshots, issuing intuitive commands, observing the outcome, and adjusting. The agent receives no robot-specific fine-tuning and no access to privileged state information: it perceives visual input and acts through a small set of general tools. VIA inherits the agent's general reasoning, closed-loop error recovery, and ability to plan and re-plan from what it observes. It solves a diverse suite of tabletop manipulation tasks zero-shot with both Claude Code and Codex. With the strongest model (Fable 5) it achieves 96.7% success on three LIBERO-Goal tasks and 100% on a long-horizon rainbow assembly task. Performance improves with the scale and strength of the underlying model. These results suggest that frontier agents already possess skills that transfer directly to robot control given the right interface: your coding or computer-use agent is, in a sense, secretly a robot-control agent.

AI.tldr: VIA is a framework that leverages off-the-shelf foundation model agents to control robots through a browser-based 3D interface, achieving 96.7% success on LIBERO-Goal tasks and 100% on a rainbow assembly task without robot-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current methods convert foundation models into vision-language-action (VLA) models via fine-tuning on limited robot data, resulting in significantly smaller models with limited capabilities. The authors explore whether frontier foundation models already possess robot control skills that can be leveraged through a proper interface.
AI.method: VIA recasts robot control as an agentic task where an off-the-shelf foundation model-powered agent drives a manipulator through a browser-based 3D interface. The agent takes screenshots, issues commands, observes outcomes, and adjusts its actions. No robot-specific fine-tuning or privileged state access is provided; the agent only uses general tools and visual input.
AI.result: VIA achieves 96.7% success on three LIBERO-Goal tasks and 100% success on a long-horizon rainbow assembly task using the Fable 5 model. Performance improves with the scale and strength of the underlying foundation model, demonstrating zero-shot transfer capability on diverse tabletop manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Frontier foundation models already possess robot control transferable skills given the right interface - coding or computer-use agents can function as robot-control agents without needing robot-specific training. This suggests a paradigm shift from fine-tuning VLAs to leveraging existing agentic capabilities through appropriate interfaces.

title: Comparison-Based Ordinal Learning for Proactive Driving Risk Assessment
summary: Real-time driving risk assessment provides an essential basis for proactive safety by identifying and quantifying the danger of ongoing road interactions before adverse outcomes occur. However, due to the scarcity of collision data and frame-level risk labels, existing driving risk assessment methods often rely on surrogate objectives, which may imperfectly align with true collision risk and not faithfully reflect the relative danger of driving interaction. This paper proposes a comparison-based ordinal risk learning framework that learns collision-relevant risk scores from pairwise supervision in driving data, directly modeling relative risk ordering without requiring numerical frame-level risk labels. We derive pairwise comparisons from three sources of event-structured driving data for such ordinal risk learning: temporal progression within safety-critical sequences, event-level contrast between dangerous and normal interactions, and physics-based counterfactual perturbations. On this basis, instantiations with three risk-scoring function parameterizations are implemented, including directly learning risk scores from comparison data, and aligning existing single or multiple surrogate-based risk models. The proposed framework is evaluated on the 100-Car and SHRP2 naturalistic driving datasets using a proactive collision warning task. Results show that the proposed framework improves high-recall risk discrimination, warning precision, and warning lead time over representative surrogate-based baselines across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations. These results suggest that the proposed framework can contribute to proactive safety research by providing more reliable risk assessment for automated driving systems and safety-critical driving interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a comparison-based ordinal risk learning framework for real-time driving risk assessment that learns collision-relevant risk scores from pairwise supervision without requiring frame-level risk labels, improving proactive safety warning performance on 100-Car and SHRP2 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing driving risk assessment methods rely on scarce collision data and frame-level risk labels, using surrogate objectives that imperfectly align with true collision risk and don't faithfully reflect relative danger of driving interactions.
AI.method: A comparison-based ordinal risk learning framework learns collision-relevant risk scores from pairwise supervision derived from three sources: temporal progression within safety-critical sequences, event-level contrast between dangerous and normal interactions, and physics-based counterfactual perturbations. Three risk-scoring function parameterizations are implemented: directly learning risk scores from comparison data, and aligning existing single or multiple surrogate-based risk models.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100-Car and SHRP2 naturalistic driving datasets using proactive collision warning task, the framework improves high-recall risk discrimination, warning precision, and warning lead time over surrogate-based baselines across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides more reliable risk assessment for automated driving systems and safety-critical driving interactions, contributing to proactive safety research by modeling relative risk ordering directly rather than relying on imperfect surrogate objectives.

title: Pix2Act: Image-Space Manipulation Policies with Equivariant Augmentation
summary: Representing manipulation actions as 2D trajectories in the camera plane provides a compact and interpretable basis for learning complex 3D manipulation policies. However, it also creates challenges from out-of-frame trajectories and limited precision. We propose Pix2Act, an imitation learning method that addresses these challenges by generating continuous image-space keypoint trajectories in each camera plane and losslessly recovering end-effector poses via triangulation. This reformulates high-dimensional 3D control as a simpler, more learnable 2D prediction problem. Crucially, it aligns observations and actions in the same coordinate space, enabling equivariant transformations to jointly rotate individual camera images together with their image-space actions. We analyze the symmetry properties of this augmentation and design a network architecture that can fuse multiple camera views while respecting their per-view rotations. As a result, Pix2Act implicitly enlarges the support of the data distribution and learns invariant action structures across transformations, yielding improved generalization and overall performance. Across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, Pix2Act outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains robust under camera perturbations.

AI.tldr: Pix2Act is an imitation learning method that represents manipulation actions as 2D trajectories in the camera plane, reformulating high-dimensional 3D control as a learnable 2D prediction problem through image-space keypoint trajectories and triangulation-based pose recovery.
AI.motivation: While representing manipulation actions as 2D trajectories provides a compact and interpretable basis for learning complex 3D manipulation policies, this approach creates challenges from out-of-frame trajectories and limited precision.
AI.method: Pix2Act addresses these challenges by: (1) generating continuous image-space keypoint trajectories in each camera plane, (2) recovering end-effector poses via triangulation, (3) aligning observations and actions in the same coordinate space to enable equivariant transformations that jointly rotate camera images with their actions, (4) analyzing symmetry properties of this augmentation, and (5) designing a network architecture that fuses multiple camera views while respecting per-view rotations.
AI.result: Pix2Act implicitly enlarges the support of the data distribution and learns invariant action structures across transformations, yielding improved generalization and overall performance. It outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation tasks and remains robust under camera perturbations.
AI.conclusion: By successfully reformulating high-dimensional 3D control as a simpler, more learnable 2D prediction problem with aligned observations and actions, Pix2Act demonstrates that this approach enables better generalization and robustness in manipulation tasks, effectively addressing the challenges of out-of-frame trajectories and limited precision inherent in 2D trajectory representations.

title: GeoGS-SLAM: Online Monocular Reconstruction Using Gaussian Splatting with Geometric Priors
summary: SLAM methods based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated impressive tracking and mapping performance, but typically require additional geometric information from external depth sensors. Meanwhile, recent SLAM systems that leverage geometric priors from pre-trained feed-forward models enable real-time dense reconstruction, yet often discard original RGB information during optimization, thus degrading overall reconstruction quality. We present GeoGS-SLAM, an online monocular dense reconstruction system that combines the 3DGS-based map representation with learned geometric priors. Given uncalibrated RGB input, we first employ a feed-forward visual geometry model to predict camera and scene priors. The Gaussian scene map is then expanded by directly sampling Gaussian primitives from both RGB input and geometric priors. Camera poses and the scene map are jointly optimized through a coarse-to-fine strategy that minimizes both photometric and geometric losses. To ensure global consistency, we further incorporate online loop closure detection and pose graph optimization. Extensive experiments across indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that GeoGS-SLAM achieves superior rendering quality and tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining online real-time performance. Project page: https://rlgao.github.io/geogs_slam.

AI.tldr: GeoGS-SLAM is an online monocular dense reconstruction system that combines 3D Gaussian Splatting with learned geometric priors, achieving superior rendering quality and tracking accuracy while maintaining real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS-based SLAM methods require additional geometric information from external depth sensors, while recent feed-forward SLAM systems that leverage geometric priors discard original RGB information during optimization, degrading reconstruction quality.
AI.method: The system employs a feed-forward visual geometry model to predict camera and scene priors from uncalibrated RGB input, expands the Gaussian scene map by sampling primitives from both RGB input and geometric priors, and jointly optimizes camera poses and scene map through a coarse-to-fine strategy minimizing photometric and geometric losses. It further incorporates online loop closure detection and pose graph optimization to ensure global consistency.
AI.result: GeoGS-SLAM achieves superior rendering quality and tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining online real-time performance across indoor and outdoor benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: By effectively combining 3DGS-based map representation with learned geometric priors, GeoGS-SLAM demonstrates that monocular dense reconstruction can achieve both high-quality results and real-time performance without requiring external depth sensors or discarding RGB information.

title: Stop to Decide: Latency-Aware Proprioceptive Navigation Primitives for Mapping-Free Quadruped Inspection
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables. Hanting Suo and Haonan Yan contributed equally. Submitted to Intelligent Service Robotics
summary: Compute-constrained quadrupeds often run their navigation loop far below the controller's design rate: sharing the onboard Jetson Orin with the vision pipeline slows our stair loop to about 15 Hz. This latency breaks a standard proprioceptive pattern: declaring stair-summit arrival from the body-pitch signal while still climbing. On a stepped platform whose 50 cm top is shorter than the robot (Unitree Go2, about 75 cm), in-motion detection overshoots the top edge with probability rising with the per-period advance v/f (the slowest about 15 Hz cell partly diluted by a separate non-arrival mode), whereas a climb-settle cadence holds overshoot near zero at every loop rate (pooled 22/45 vs 1/45 over about 30/20/15 Hz; Fisher p about 2.4e-7; 7/15 vs 0/15 at the deployed about 15 Hz). A logistic dose-response model in v/f captures the failure; a pre-specified 40 Hz out-of-sample test favours the protocol-clean fit (33% observed vs 43%/22% predicted), giving a deployment rule (critical loop rate about 19 Hz at 0.30 m/s). The detector sits in a fully onboard, mapping-free and learning-free stack: built-in inertial measurement unit, four foot-force channels, three 1-D ranges, one line camera, chaining line-following, a three-segment maneuver for 90-degree corners in a 55 cm corridor (20/20 contact-free vs 14/20 with 12 wall contacts for in-place yaw; exit-heading error 1.56 degrees vs 5.64 degrees), and stair traversal, completing the inspection course in 18/20 trials (90%). Results are from a single course geometry, platform, and operator.

AI.tldr: A compute-constrained quadruped (Unitree Go2) with a 15 Hz navigation loop experiences stair-summit detection failures due to latency; a climb-settle cadence reduces overshoot from 48.9% to 2.2% at 15 Hz, with a deployment rule of ~19 Hz critical loop rate at 0.30 m/s, enabling 90% course completion using onboard sensors.
AI.motivation: Compute-constrained quadrupeds (e.g., Jetson Orin) running navigation loops at low frequencies (e.g., 15 Hz) cause latency that breaks proprioceptive stair-summit detection, leading to overshoot when climbing platforms shorter than the robot height.
AI.method: Compared in-motion detection vs. climb-settle cadence on a stepped platform (50 cm top, 75 cm robot height) across loop rates (30/20/15 Hz). Used logistic dose-response model with v/f ratio to capture failure probability. Out-of-sample test at 40 Hz. Evaluated line-following, 90° corner navigation, and stair traversal.
AI.result: Climb-settle cadence reduces stair-summit overshoot to near zero (1/45 vs 22/45) across loop rates, logistic model fits failure well, and 40 Hz out-of-sample test shows 33% observed vs 43%/22% predicted. Deployment rule: ~19 Hz critical loop rate at 0.30 m/s. Course completion: 90% (18/20 trials).
AI.conclusion: Latency-induced stair-summit detection failure can be mitigated by using a climb-settle cadence instead of in-motion detection, with a practical deployment threshold of ~19 Hz loop rate at 0.30 m/s, enabling robust stair traversal without vision or mapping.

title: Towards Predictive, Aligned, and Scalable Robot Learning
summary: Learning, at its core, extends beyond memorization to the ability to reason and solve novel problems by navigating a space of possibilities. We introduce Lumo-2, a latent world-action model that generates actions by reasoning over world dynamics in latent space. The learned latent world dynamics capture physically grounded visual transitions, naturally encoding future possibilities and providing a unified substrate for cross-modal alignment. This formulation enables predictive reasoning akin to world modelling while remaining lightweight and focused on physical dynamics relevant to control. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that action generation quality is governed by the geometry of the latent space. We observe that standard reconstruction-based action tokenization objectives induce representations biased toward low-level signal fidelity, leading to misalignment between reconstruction quality and downstream control performance. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-stage modality pre-alignment strategy in which action representations are progressively aligned with latent world dynamics, vision, and language. This process enforces cross-modal consistency, promotes abstraction, and induces a structured latent space for predictive reasoning. We provide a systematic empirical study of latent world modelling and modality alignment, analyzing their roles in scaling laws and out-of-distribution generalization. Results show that Lumo-2 consistently outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) baselines, with gains on challenging real-world tasks requiring temporal reasoning, physical understanding, or high control complexity, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation. These findings suggest that structured multimodal alignment and predictive reasoning are fundamental principles for advancing embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: Lumo-2 is a latent world-action model that generates actions by reasoning over world dynamics in latent space, employing a multi-stage modality pre-alignment strategy to address low-level signal fidelity bias in standard action tokenization objectives.
AI.motivation: Learning should extend beyond memorization to reasoning and solving novel problems. Standard reconstruction-based action tokenization induces representations biased toward low-level signal fidelity, leading to misalignment between reconstruction quality and downstream control performance. The authors hypothesize that action generation quality is governed by the geometry of the latent space.
AI.method: Lumo-2 introduces a latent world-action model that generates actions by reasoning over world dynamics in latent space. It employs a multi-stage modality pre-alignment strategy that progressively aligns action representations with latent world dynamics, vision, and language. This process enforces cross-modal consistency, promotes abstraction, and induces a structured latent space for predictive reasoning.
AI.result: Lumo-2 consistently outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) baselines, with gains on challenging real-world tasks requiring temporal reasoning, physical understanding, or high control complexity, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Structured multimodal alignment and predictive reasoning are fundamental principles for advancing embodied intelligence. The findings suggest that properly structured latent spaces and cross-modal consistency are critical for effective world modelling and action generation.

title: CR-Solver: GPU-Accelerated Kinematics Solver for Tendon-driven Continuum Robots
summary: Continuum robots provide intrinsic compliance, high dexterity, and safe physical interaction, enabling navigation and manipulation in confined and unstructured environments. Despite recent advances in sensing and control, heightening the need for precise motion generation, most widely used planning libraries are grounded in rigid-body assumptions, creating a critical gap for fast and practical tools for continuum robots. To address this, we present CR-Solver, a two-stage, optimization-based solver for the motion generation of tendon-driven continuum robots. Our method unifies inverse kinematics, path following, and trajectory planning within a single constrained nonlinear optimization framework. Leveraging GPU-accelerated parallel optimization, CR-Solver delivers fast, accurate, and constraint-aware solutions. We validate our approach on three tasks, demonstrating significant speedups over traditional CPU-based solvers while achieving a consistently high success rate above 95% and millimeter-level accuracy. The solver is implemented in pure Python, reducing the barrier to adoption and offering a practical, extensible foundation for continuum robots' high-performance motion planning.

AI.tldr: CR-Solver is a two-stage optimization-based solver for tendon-driven continuum robots that unifies inverse kinematics, path following, and trajectory planning in a single constrained nonlinear optimization framework, implemented in pure Python with GPU acceleration.
AI.motivation: Continuum robots offer intrinsic compliance, high dexterity, and safe interaction for navigation/manipulation in confined/unstructured environments. However, most widely used planning libraries are grounded in rigid-body assumptions, creating a critical gap for fast, practical motion generation tools specifically designed for continuum robots.
AI.method: CR-Solver employs a two-stage optimization-based approach that unifies inverse kinematics, path following, and trajectory planning within a single constrained nonlinear optimization framework. The method leverages GPU-accelerated parallel optimization for fast computation and is implemented in pure Python to reduce adoption barriers.
AI.result: Validation across three tasks demonstrates significant speedups over traditional CPU-based solvers while achieving consistently high success rates above 95% and millimeter-level accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CR-Solver provides a practical, extensible foundation for continuum robots' high-performance motion planning with reduced implementation barriers through its pure Python implementation.

title: A Glimpse into Long-term Physical Coexistence with Intelligent Robots
summary: Long-term physical coexistence with intelligent robots requires more than capable robot policies. A persistent robotic assistant must support diverse user-facing interfaces, maintain long-horizon memory of people and preferences, coordinate across robot embodiments, and translate human intent into safe physical execution. We introduce PHILIA, a multi-robot agent built around a robot gateway abstraction. PHILIA retains the rich interaction and tool ecosystem of OpenClaw while exposing robot-local runtimes, onboard perception, navigation, speaker, and robot policies through a unified capability interface. This design decouples low-frequency, high-semantic agent reasoning from high-frequency, low-level robot execution, enabling plug-and-play integration of user interfaces, robot embodiments, and policy backends. As a result, the user experience becomes compositional: advances in user interfaces, robot embodiments, robot policies, navigation, or interaction algorithms can improve the overall experience without redesigning the system. We validate the architecture on Astribot S1 robots while designing the robot gateway contract to support future heterogeneous robot platforms through a shared capability interface for observation, task execution, navigation, speech playback, status monitoring, and task cancellation. We present representative use cases in which agent memory and scene understanding are grounded in robot actions. These span interactive household scenarios, ranging from simple organization to challenging long-horizon and dexterous service tasks, such as packing a backpack and lifting a garbage bag. We highlight the human-robot interaction flow, where contextual understanding of user intent and preferences, together with human-in-the-loop confirmation or adjustment during execution, is essential for effective assistance.

AI.tldr: PHILIA is a multi-robot agent system that enables long-term human-robot coexistence through a robot gateway abstraction, decoupling high-level agent reasoning from low-level robot execution for compositional system architecture.
AI.motivation: Long-term physical coexistence with intelligent robots requires more than capable robot policies. A persistent robotic assistant must support diverse user-facing interfaces, maintain long-horizon memory of people and preferences, coordinate across robot embodiments, and translate human intent into safe physical execution.
AI.method: PHILIA is built around a robot gateway abstraction that exposes robot-local runtimes, onboard perception, navigation, speaker, and robot policies through a unified capability interface. This design decouples low-frequency, high-semantic agent reasoning from high-frequency, low-level robot execution, enabling plug-and-play integration of user interfaces, robot embodiments, and policy backends.
AI.result: The architecture was validated on Astribot S1 robots with a robot gateway contract supporting observation, task execution, navigation, speech playback, status monitoring, and task cancellation. Representative use cases demonstrated interactive household scenarios ranging from simple organization to challenging long-horizon and dexterous service tasks like packing a backpack and lifting a garbage bag.
AI.conclusion: The compositional design allows advances in different system components to improve the overall experience without redesigning the entire system. Human-robot interaction flows with contextual understanding and human-in-the-loop confirmation are essential for effective assistance, with agent memory and scene understanding grounded in robot actions.

title: From Sketch Prior to Trajectories: A Mission-Oriented Coordinated Navigation Framework for Indoor UAV Swarm
summary: UAV swarm for applications, such as indoor inspection, security patrol, and logistics delivery, are often mission-oriented rather than exploration-oriented. In these tasks, UAVs are required to visit task-relevant regions in a prescribed sequence, and such region-level mission information can often be obtained from pre-deployment sketch-map priors, such as floor plans, CAD layouts, or evacuation diagrams. Although these tasks are executed in three-dimensional space, UAVs usually fly within a specific altitude layer or a nearly fixed altitude range on each floor, making mission-level region transitions mainly governed by planar connectivity. Based on these observations, this paper proposes a mission-oriented coordinated navigation framework that exploits sketch-map priors for multi-UAV indoor operations. Onboard observations are used to perform topological alignment, and the aligned prior is fused with online observations to construct a mission-oriented traversability representation. A layered 2D--3D coordinated navigation framework is further developed, where 2D guided path planning generates mission-oriented guide paths and guide-driven 3D trajectory optimization produces dynamically feasible and collision-free trajectories. Simulation and real-world experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in structured multi-room indoor environments and further demonstrate its coordinated navigation capability under both communication-available and communication-loss conditions. Multi-floor simulation results show the scalability of the system to layered indoor structures.

AI.tldr: A mission-oriented coordinated navigation framework for UAV swarms in indoor environments that exploits sketch-map priors (floor plans, CAD layouts) for multi-UAV operations, combining topological alignment, traversability representation, and a layered 2D-3D navigation approach.
AI.motivation: UAV swarms for indoor tasks (inspection, security, logistics) are mission-oriented rather than exploration-oriented, requiring visitation of task-relevant regions in prescribed sequences. While operating in 3D, UAVs typically fly at specific altitude layers per floor, making planar connectivity the main factor for region transitions. Existing methods may not effectively leverage pre-deployment sketch-map priors for mission-oriented navigation.
AI.method: Uses onboard observations for topological alignment to align sketch-map priors with online observations, constructing a mission-oriented traversability representation. Develops a layered 2D-3D coordinated navigation framework where 2D guided path planning generates mission-oriented guide paths and guide-driven 3D trajectory optimization produces dynamically feasible and collision-free trajectories.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments validate effectiveness in structured multi-room indoor environments, demonstrating coordinated navigation capability under both communication-available and communication-loss conditions. Multi-floor simulation results show scalability to layered indoor structures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively leverages sketch-map priors for multi-UAV indoor operations, combining 2D-3D coordinated navigation to achieve robust mission-oriented navigation in structured environments, with demonstrated scalability and resilience to communication challenges.

title: WALA Learning Executable Latent Actions from Action-Labeled Demonstrations and Action-Free Videos
summary: Generalizable robot policies typically rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations, which are expensive to collect and difficult to scale. In contrast, large-scale human and robot videos contain rich physical interactions but often lack executable robot action labels. We present WALA, a framework for learning executable latent actions from both action-labeled demonstrations and action-free videos. WALA first pretrains a semantic-geometric latent action model from videos by modeling the evolution between current observations and sparsely sampled future observations.
