Instead of reconstructing raw pixels, WALA predicts future deltas in the DINOv3 feature space and dense depth space, preserving task-relevant semantic and geometric structure while reducing sensitivity to appearance details. During policy training, the pretrained encoder provides stable latent action targets, and the decoder serves as a trainable latent world model. The latent actions generated by the vision-language backbone are jointly supervised by robot action prediction, latent action target matching, and future dynamics prediction. This enables action-labeled demonstrations to provide executable control supervision, while action-free videos contribute dynamics supervision without requiring robot action annotations. Experiments show that WALA achieves strong performance on RoboTwin, sets a new state-of-the-art result on RoboCasa with 75.2% average success, and improves both policy performance and generalization in real-world manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: WALA learns executable latent actions from both action-labeled demonstrations and action-free videos by pretraining a semantic-geometric latent action model that predicts future deltas in DINOv3 feature space and depth space, enabling joint supervision through robot action prediction, latent action target matching, and future dynamics prediction.
AI.motivation: Generalizable robot policies typically rely on expensive-to-collect action-labeled robot demonstrations that are difficult to scale. In contrast, large-scale human and robot videos contain rich physical interactions but lack executable robot action labels.
AI.method: WALA pretrains a semantic-geometric latent action model from videos by modeling evolution between current and future observations, predicting future deltas in DINOv3 feature space and dense depth space (rather than raw pixels). During policy training, the pretrained encoder provides stable latent action targets while the decoder serves as a trainable latent world model. The latent actions are jointly supervised by robot action prediction, latent action target matching, and future dynamics prediction.
AI.result: WALA achieves strong performance on RoboTwin, sets a new state-of-the-art result on RoboCasa with 75.2% average success, and improves both policy performance and generalization in real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: WALA enables learning executable latent actions from both action-labeled demonstrations and action-free videos, achieving superior performance and generalization in robot manipulation tasks by effectively combining control supervision from labeled data with dynamics supervision from unlabeled videos.

title: EDAR: Learning Environment-Dependent Action Representations for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Learning effective action representations is critical for robotic manipulation, where raw control trajectories are often noisy, redundant, and difficult to model directly. Existing methods mainly encode the structure of the action stream itself, treating the role of actions in the environment as implicit. Yet manipulation is about changing the world: the same action segment can induce different outcomes under different scene contexts, making action semantics inherently environment-dependent. We propose EDAR, an Environment-Dependent Action Representation that grounds action tokens in both executable control structure and expected visual consequences. By coupling motor commands with their environment-conditioned effects, EDAR encourages the learned action space to capture interaction semantics rather than merely command-level patterns. Experiments on simulated and real-robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that EDAR improves downstream policy learning, especially in long-horizon manipulation. These results highlight the importance of grounding action representations in executable control structure and environment-conditioned visual change.

AI.tldr: EDAR (Environment-Dependent Action Representation) grounds action tokens in both executable control structure and expected visual consequences, coupling motor commands with environment-conditioned effects to capture interaction semantics rather than just command-level patterns.
AI.motivation: Raw control trajectories are noisy, redundant, and difficult to model directly. Existing methods encode action stream structure while treating the role of actions in the environment as implicit. However, manipulation is about changing the world—same action segments can induce different outcomes under different scene contexts, making action semantics inherently environment-dependent.
AI.method: EDAR (Environment-Dependent Action Representation) grounds action tokens in both executable control structure and expected visual consequences by coupling motor commands with their environment-conditioned effects, encouraging the learned action space to capture interaction semantics rather than merely command-level patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated and real-robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that EDAR improves downstream policy learning, especially for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: These results highlight the critical importance of grounding action representations in executable control structure and environment-conditioned visual change for effective robotic manipulation.

title: Towards Human-level Dexterous Teleoperation
summary: Humans routinely wield tools, swap grasps, and reposition objects within a single hand, seamlessly orchestrating contact transitions that span translation, reorientation, and finger gaiting. Endowing robot dexterous hands with this level of in-hand dexterity through teleoperation requires precise control of object motion via dynamic hand-object contact, yet current teleoperation systems remain far from this capability. To bridge this gap, we take a major step towards human-level dexterous teleoperation by introducing TeleDexter, a hand-object co-tracking controller that maps operator intent into learned, low-level contact execution. The controller is trained on consecutive co-tracking subgoals derived from human reference motions, utilizing a hybrid reward that couples sparse subgoal objectives with dense tracking rewards to enable learning across diverse interaction modalities rather than frame-wise trajectory imitation. The entire pipeline requires only single-stage RL and, with random action masking and domain randomization, transfers zero-shot to the real robot. We evaluate TeleDexter on seven challenging dexterous teleoperation tasks spanning object reorientation and long-horizon tool use across two dexterous hands, achieving a 75% average success rate where all baselines consistently fail. Furthermore, the collected demonstrations successfully train autonomous policies via behavioral cloning, marking a concrete step towards human-level dexterous teleoperation.

AI.tldr: TeleDexter is a dexterous teleoperation system that enables robot hands to perform complex in-hand manipulation tasks by mapping operator intent to learned contact execution through hand-object co-tracking, achieving 75% average success rate across seven challenging tasks where baselines fail.
AI.motivation: Humans seamlessly orchestrate complex contact transitions (translation, reorientation, finger gaiting) when using tools, but current teleoperation systems cannot achieve this level of dexterity, creating a gap in enabling robot hands to perform human-level in-hand manipulation.
AI.method: TeleDexter employs a hand-object co-tracking controller trained on consecutive co-tracking subgoals derived from human reference motions using a hybrid reward combining sparse subgoal objectives with dense tracking rewards. The system requires only single-stage RL with random action masking and domain randomization for zero-shot transfer to real robots.
AI.result: TeleDexter achieves 75% average success rate on seven challenging dexterous teleoperation tasks spanning object reorientation and long-horizon tool use across two dexterous hands, outperforming all baselines. The collected demonstrations can successfully train autonomous policies via behavioral cloning.
AI.conclusion: TeleDexter represents a major step towards human-level dexterous teleoperation, bridging the capability gap between current systems and human manipulation dexterity through learned contact execution rather than frame-wise trajectory imitation.

title: See like a Robot: Robot-Centric Pointmaps for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. These actions are defined in the robot's own 3D coordinate frame, yet most VLAs observe the scene in the camera frame, creating a frame mismatch between where the scene is observed and where actions are defined. The mismatch is benign under a fixed viewpoint, where the policy can memorize a single observation-to-action mapping, but grows harder as large-scale datasets aggregate demonstrations across diverse camera setups and the policy must generalize this mapping across viewpoints. We address this mismatch with robot-centric pointmaps, images whose pixels store the 3D coordinates of scene points in the robot frame. Pointmaps provide robot-frame 3D geometry while preserving the dense H x W grid expected by pretrained 2D VLAs, so they integrate into existing VLAs with minimal architectural change. On RoboCasa, pointmaps improve both pi0.5 and SmolVLA and outperform representative camera-viewpoint and 3D-aware baselines. In real-robot experiments, their advantage over an RGB-only policy widens when the camera is moved to a placement unseen during training.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces robot-centric pointmaps to address the frame mismatch problem in vision-language-action (VLA) models, where actions are defined in the robot's 3D coordinate frame while visual observations are typically in the camera frame. Pointmaps store 3D scene coordinates in the robot frame within a dense HxW grid, enabling pretrained 2D VLAs to operate with robot-frame geometry.
AI.motivation: VLA models predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. Actions are defined in the robot's 3D coordinate frame, yet most VLAs observe scenes in the camera frame, creating a frame mismatch. This mismatch is manageable with fixed viewpoints (single observation-to-action mapping) but becomes problematic with large-scale datasets across diverse camera setups requiring generalization across viewpoints.
AI.method: The authors introduce robot-centric pointmaps—images where pixels store the 3D coordinates of scene points in the robot frame. These provide robot-frame 3D geometry while preserving the dense HxW grid expected by pretrained 2D VLAs, allowing integration with minimal architectural changes.
AI.result: On the RoboCasa dataset, pointmaps improve both pi0.5 and SmolVLA, outperforming representative camera-viewpoint and 3D-aware baselines. In real-robot experiments, the advantage over RGB-only policies widens when the camera is placed in positions unseen during training.
AI.conclusion: Robot-centric pointmaps effectively address the frame mismatch in VLA models, enabling better generalization across diverse camera setups and improving performance, particularly in out-of-distribution camera placement scenarios.

title: ERR@HRI 3.0 Challenge: Multimodal Detection of Errors and Anticipation in Human-Robot Interactions
summary: As robots become increasingly integrated into human environments, their ability to detect and respond to errors remains critical for maintaining user trust and interaction quality. While recent advances in machine learning have improved error detection capabilities, most approaches are limited to specific contexts, controlled settings, or pre-extracted features, limiting their generalizability and applicability to real-world conditions. To address this challenge, the third edition of the ERR@HRI Challenge (ERR@HRI 3.0) provided researchers with two complementary datasets that enable end-to-end innovation in methods for both detecting and preventing errors in human-robot interaction. The challenge offered raw, non-anonymized video data from naturalistic settings: (1) the Bystander Affect Detection (BAD) dataset, containing webcam recordings of 45 participants' spontaneous reactions to robot and human failure scenarios; and (2) the Bad Idea dataset, featuring 29 participants' anticipatory facial responses while predicting action outcomes before failures occur. Both datasets were collected via crowdsourcing, capturing the inherent variability of real-world conditions. This naturalistic variability, while challenging, provides an authentic testbed for developing robust error detection systems. Participants developed multimodal machine learning models for bystander reaction detection (Track 1) and anticipatory outcome prediction (Track 2), with an optional cross-dataset generalization track (Track 3). Three teams submitted valid models, all of which surpassed our convolutional neural network baselines. This paper describes the datasets, tasks, baselines, and results of ERR@HRI 3.0, and discusses implications for building generalizable, context-aware, and anticipatory error detection systems for human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: ERR@HRI 3.0 is a challenge providing two naturalistic video datasets (BAD and Bad Idea) and tasks for developing error detection and prevention systems in human-robot interaction. Three teams submitted models that surpassed CNN baselines.
AI.motivation: As robots integrate into human environments, error detection is critical for maintaining user trust and interaction quality. Existing ML approaches are limited to specific contexts, controlled settings, or pre-extracted features, lacking generalizability for real-world applications.
AI.method: Provided two crowdsourced naturalistic video datasets: BAD (45 participants' spontaneous reactions to robot/human failure via webcam) and Bad Idea (29 participants' anticipatory facial responses predicting outcomes). Tasks included bystander reaction detection, anticipatory outcome prediction, and cross-dataset generalization. Used CNN baselines for comparison.
AI.result: Three teams submitted valid models, all of which surpassed the CNN baseline performance across the challenge tracks.
AI.conclusion: Naturalistic variability provides an authentic testbed for developing robust error detection systems. The results demonstrate potential for building generalizable, context-aware, and anticipatory error detection systems in HRI.

title: WarpMPC: Large-Batch MPC on GPU via ADMM with Unrolled $LDL^\top$ Factorization
summary: This paper introduces numerical optimizations for maximizing throughput on GPU when solving large batches (10,000 to over 100,000) of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations, where all problems have the same structure. The optimizations are implemented in a toolbox WarpMPC for model-predictive control (MPC) in JAX and Warp. Based on the insight that all MPC problem instances in a batch share the same sparsity in time, cost, and constraints, we propose unrolling sparse linear factorizations and solves, which dominate alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver runtime. We avoid memory access bottlenecks and wasting computations via optimized memory layout, padding-reducing segmentation of the unrolled factorization, and dependency level scheduled backsolves, additionally accelerating sensitivity computation. We achieve throughputs of 8,000 to 250,000 SQP iterations per second on nonlinear cartpole, quadrotor, and humanoid robot benchmarks, outperforming baselines by 3$\times$ to 25$\times$. We illustrate practical usefulness by synthesizing a dataset and training a neural network approximation of an MPC in under 4 minutes that stabilizes a nano quadrotor in hardware experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GPU-accelerated numerical optimizations for large-batch sequential quadratic programming (SQP) in the WarpMPC toolbox, achieving 8,000-250,000 SQP iterations/second on robot benchmarks by unrolling sparse linear factorizations and optimizing memory layouts, with 3-25× speedup over baselines.
AI.motivation: Solving large batches (10,000-100,000+) of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations for model-predictive control (MPC) on GPUs faces throughput bottlenecks due to shared sparsity patterns across problem instances and inefficient memory access patterns.
AI.method: The authors leverage the insight that all MPC instances share sparsity in time, cost, and constraints to unroll sparse linear factorizations and solves (dominating ADMM runtime). Key optimizations include: 1) optimized memory layout to avoid bottlenecks, 2) padding-reducing segmentation of unrolled factorization, 3) dependency-level scheduled backsolves, 4) acceleration of sensitivity computation. Implemented in WarpMPC toolbox for MPC in JAX and Warp.
AI.result: Achieved throughputs of 8,000 to 250,000 SQP iterations per second on nonlinear cartpole, quadrotor, and humanoid robot benchmarks, outperforming baselines by 3× to 25×. Successfully synthesized a dataset and trained a neural network approximation of MPC in under 4 minutes, demonstrating hardware stabilization of a nano quadrotor.
AI.conclusion: The proposed optimizations effectively address GPU throughput limitations for large-batch SQP, enabling practical applications like rapid MPC neural network training and real-time hardware stabilization, demonstrating both computational efficiency and practical utility in robot control.

title: SKooP: Symmetric Koopman Predictions for Faster and More Generalizable Legged Robot Locomotion with Reinforcement Learning
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), Pittsburgh, USA, 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms classically suffer from poor sample efficiency. In robotics, a recent line of work has emerged addressing this problem by encoding physics priors in the learning process. However, most of these approaches are validated on well-defined, low-dimensional benchmark systems rather than high-dimensional robots with complex nonlinear dynamics. In this paper, we introduce \textit{SKooP (Symmetric Koopman Predictions)}, an approach combining the advantages of morphological symmetries with those of a Koopman model learned via autoencoder to enhance policy learning. SKooP learns a Koopman model of the system dynamics alongside the policy. The resulting Koopman predictions are used as privileged observations for the critic, allowing the agent to learn based on smoother, more informative features. We also incorporate group symmetries into the actor, critic, encoder and decoder networks to produce a highly equivariant policy. The SKooP approach is validated via in-depth analysis of the learned Koopman models and symmetric policies to showcase how each of these influences the agent's performance. We also show that the learned policies are transferable to different simulation environments. Our results show that SKooP consistently reduces convergence time and increases the learned reward for multiple challenging bipedal locomotion tasks on a quadruped robot. Project page: https://evelyd.github.io/SymmetricKoopmanPredictions/

AI.tldr: SKooP (Symmetric Koopman Predictions) combines morphological symmetries with Koopman autoencoder models to improve sample efficiency in RL for robotics, achieving faster convergence and higher rewards on bipedal locomotion tasks.
AI.motivation: RL algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency in robotics. While physics-informed approaches exist, most are validated on low-dimensional benchmarks rather than high-dimensional robots with complex nonlinear dynamics.
AI.method: SKooP learns a Koopman model of system dynamics alongside the policy using an autoencoder. It incorporates group symmetries into actor, critic, encoder, and decoder networks to produce equivariant policies. Koopman predictions serve as privileged observations for the critic.
AI.result: SKooP consistently reduces convergence time and increases learned reward for multiple bipedal locomotion tasks on a quadruped robot. The learned policies are transferable to different simulation environments.
AI.conclusion: By combining morphological symmetries with Koopman autoencoders, SKooP provides a principled approach to enhance sample efficiency in high-dimensional robotic systems, validated through in-depth analysis of learned models and policies.

title: Breaking the 15% Barrier: A Real-World Data-Driven System for Proactive Social Robot Triggered by User Nonverbal Cues
comment: 8 pages, accepted as a conference paper for IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS2026)
summary: Service robots in retail stores increasingly rely on cascaded speech pipelines (STT-LLM-TTS), yet many customer-robot interactions are initiated or guided by nonverbal behaviors such as approaching, waving, pointing, or showing items. This paper studies such cues in a real-world store deployment with a teleoperated humanoid robot and shows that a non-negligible portion of robot turns are triggered by nonverbal behaviors rather than spoken input, revealing a limitation of audio-only dialogue systems. In a 6-day in-the-wild deployment, 15.3\% of robot utterances were initiated by users' nonverbal behaviors rather than spoken input. Based on an analysis of observed customer behaviors, we define a set of frequent, service-relevant nonverbal cues and develop a real-time multi-person, multi-label recognizer that runs online from video. We then propose a dialogue framework that conditions LLM-based utterance generation on recognized nonverbal cue tokens, and optionally leverages a vision-language model when items are shown, enabling proactive robot responses without hand-crafted rules. We evaluate the approach offline on nonverbal-triggered turns and demonstrate an online prototype that reacts to users' nonverbal cues in real time.

AI.tldr: A 6-day real-world retail deployment shows that 15.3% of robot utterances are triggered by nonverbal behaviors (approaching, waving, pointing, showing items) rather than spoken input. The paper introduces a real-time multi-person nonverbal recognizer and a dialogue framework that conditions LLM generation on these cues, enabling proactive responses without hand-crafted rules.
AI.motivation: Service robots in retail increasingly use cascaded speech pipelines (STT-LLM-TTS), but many customer interactions are initiated by nonverbal behaviors such as approaching, waving, pointing, or showing items. This reveals a limitation of audio-only dialogue systems.
AI.method: 1. Conducted 6-day in-the-wild deployment with teleoperated humanoid robot to analyze customer behaviors; 2. Defined frequent service-relevant nonverbal cues; 3. Developed a real-time multi-person, multi-label recognizer from video; 4. Proposed a dialogue framework that conditions LLM-based utterance generation on recognized nonverbal cues; 5. Optionally leveraged a vision-language model when items are shown; 6. Evaluated offline on nonverbal-triggered turns and demonstrated an online prototype.
AI.result: 15.3% of robot utterances were initiated by users' nonverbal behaviors rather than spoken input in the 6-day deployment. The approach was evaluated offline and demonstrated via an online prototype that reacts to nonverbal cues in real time.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating nonverbal behavior recognition significantly improves service robot dialogue systems by enabling them to respond to customer cues like approaching, waving, pointing, and showing items, reducing reliance on audio-only input and enabling proactive responses without hand-crafted rules.

title: DA-Nav: Direction-Aware City-Scale Vision-Language Navigation
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: City-scale outdoor navigation is currently hindered by the heavy reliance on dense maps or costly navigation supervision. In this work, we introduce a novel paradigm for leveraging directional instructions from commercial navigation tools (e.g., Google Maps). To bridge the gap between commercial instructions and executable navigation actions, while mitigating long-horizon error accumulation through robust trajectory recovery, we propose DA-Nav, a Direction-Aware vision-language Navigation framework that reformulates navigation as a discrete spatial grounding problem on the egocentric 2D image plane. To achieve trajectory recovery, DA-Nav employs a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning process encompassing deviation assessment, action prediction, and target grid selection. We further introduce ReDA, a dataset that provides direction-aware instructions and recovery trajectories to enhance spatial grounding and support CoT recovery reasoning. Extensive experiments in CARLA demonstrate that DA-Nav achieves a high success rate of 56.16% in unseen urban environments, outperforming existing State-of-The-Art (SoTA) methods while maintaining a substantially stronger recovery capability. Furthermore, without fine-tuning, DA-Nav seamlessly adapts to both quadruped and humanoid robots, enabling stable kilometer-scale closed-loop outdoor navigation in complex real world environments.

AI.tldr: DA-Nav is a Direction-Aware vision-language Navigation framework that reformulates outdoor navigation as a discrete spatial grounding problem on egocentric 2D images, employing Chain-of-Thought reasoning for trajectory recovery. It achieves 56.16% success rate on unseen urban environments and enables kilometer-scale closed-loop navigation without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: City-scale outdoor navigation is hindered by heavy reliance on dense maps or costly navigation supervision. There is a gap between commercial navigation instructions (e.g., Google Maps) and executable navigation actions, and long-horizon error accumulation remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: DA-Nav reformulates navigation as a discrete spatial grounding problem on the egocentric 2D image plane. It employs Chain-of-Thought reasoning encompassing deviation assessment, action prediction, and target grid selection. Additionally, it introduces ReDA, a dataset providing direction-aware instructions and recovery trajectories.
AI.result: DA-Nav achieves 56.16% success rate in unseen urban environments in CARLA simulations, outperforming existing SoTA methods with stronger recovery capability. Without fine-tuning, it adapts to both quadruped and humanoid robots, enabling stable kilometer-scale closed-loop outdoor navigation in complex real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: DA-Nav demonstrates an effective paradigm for outdoor navigation without dense maps, showing strong generalization across robot platforms and practical applicability in complex real-world scenarios. The approach bridges the gap between commercial navigation instructions and executable actions while mitigating long-horizon error accumulation through robust trajectory recovery.

title: Xiaomi-Robotics-U0: Unified Embodied Synthesis with World Foundation Model
summary: Recent foundation image and video generation models offer strong generalization and controllability, but their direct application to embodied scenarios is limited by requirements for multi-view consistency, geometric coherence, and robot embodiment constraints. Existing methods typically adapt foundation models with limited robot data, often sacrificing visual knowledge acquired during large-scale pre-training. We present Xiaomi-Robotics-U0, a 38-billion-parameter multimodal autoregressive model for unified embodied synthesis. It treats embodied generation as an extension of foundation image and video generation and jointly optimizes text-to-image generation, image editing, embodied scene generation, embodied transfer, and embodied video generation. This unified framework preserves the generalization of the pre-trained world foundation model while adapting it to embodied settings. Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 is the first model to support high-quality multi-view scene generation across multiple robot embodiments and to introduce structured, controllable embodied transfer for fine-grained editing while preserving multi-view consistency and interaction dynamics. It achieves state-of-the-art results on single-step and sequential generation tasks, outperforming GPT-Image-2.0 in human evaluations of embodied scene generation and transfer, ranking first on World Arena for embodied video generation, and improving the out-of-distribution success rate of pi_0.5 from 36.9% to 63.2% on challenging real-world manipulation tasks. These results show that foundation world models can serve both as embodied world models and scalable data engines for embodied intelligence. Code and checkpoints are available at https://robotics.xiaomi.com/xiaomi-robotics-u0.html.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 is a 38-billion-parameter multimodal autoregressive model for unified embodied synthesis that extends foundation image/video generation to robot embodiment scenarios, jointly optimizing text-to-image, image editing, embodied scene generation, transfer, and video generation while preserving pre-trained visual knowledge.
AI.motivation: Foundation image and video generation models have strong generalization and controllability, but their direct application to embodied scenarios is limited by requirements for multi-view consistency, geometric coherence, and robot embodiment constraints. Existing methods adapt foundation models using limited robot data, often sacrificing the visual knowledge acquired during large-scale pre-training.
AI.method: Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 treats embodied generation as an extension of foundation image and video generation and jointly optimizes five tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, embodied scene generation, embodied transfer, and embodied video generation within a unified framework. This approach preserves the generalization of the pre-trained world foundation model while adapting it to embodied settings.
AI.result: Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 achieves state-of-the-art results on single-step and sequential generation tasks, outperforms GPT-Image-2.0 in human evaluations of embodied scene generation and transfer, ranks first on World Arena for embodied video generation, and improves pi_0.5's out-of-distribution success rate from 36.9% to 63.2% on challenging real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Foundation world models can serve both as embodied world models and scalable data engines for embodied intelligence, enabling high-quality multi-view scene generation across multiple robot embodiments with structured, controllable embodied transfer that preserves multi-view consistency and interaction dynamics.

title: Coordinated Incremental Trajectory Tracking of a Tailsitter Drone
summary: This paper derives an analytical differential flatness transform for a tailsitter Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) under coordinated flight conditions using a simplified aerodynamic model. The proposed framework is formulated exclusively using rotation matrices, avoiding the ambiguities inherent to Euler angle representations. The method extends the applicability of an existing state-of-the-art differential flatness-based controller to flight regimes involving a significant vertical velocity component, where the previous approach becomes inapplicable. The proposed framework is validated experimentally with trajectories that highlight its advantages in these regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an analytical differential flatness transform for a tailsitter UAV using rotation matrices (avoiding Euler angle ambiguities) to extend an existing controller's applicability to flight with significant vertical velocity, validated experimentally.
AI.motivation: To extend the applicability of an existing differential flatness-based controller to tailsitter UAV flight regimes involving a significant vertical velocity component, where the previous approach becomes inapplicable.
AI.method: Derives an analytical differential flatness transform for a tailsitter UAV under coordinated flight conditions using a simplified aerodynamic model. The framework is formulated exclusively using rotation matrices to avoid Euler angle representation ambiguities.
AI.result: The proposed framework successfully extends the state-of-the-art differential flatness-based controller to regimes with significant vertical velocity. Experimental validation with trajectories demonstrates the advantages of this approach in these flight regimes.
AI.conclusion: The analytical differential flatness transform based on rotation matrices provides a robust solution for tailsitter UAV control in flight regimes with substantial vertical velocity components, overcoming the limitations of previous Euler angle-based approaches.

title: A Model for Mediating Multi-Modal Human Intent into Safe Maneuvers for UAVs
summary: Direct human interaction with autonomous UAV systems can be enabled through modalities such as speech, gestures, and graphical interfaces. However, interpreting such inputs as directly executable commands introduces safety risks in dynamic environments. Operator requests may conflict with terrain constraints, inter-UAV separation requirements, or flight-envelope limitations. In this paper, we present a requirements-governed maneuver-response model that mediates multi-modal human intent into safe UAV maneuvers by treating operator inputs as bounded maneuver requests rather than direct commands. Requested maneuvers are mapped to constrained motion primitives and processed through a structured request-evaluate-execute pipeline. Each request is interpreted with associated confidence, validated against terrain, separation, workspace, and flight-envelope constraints, and either constrained, rejected, or executed under continuous runtime monitoring. We further formalize the approach as a requirements-based specification model in which maneuver primitives are associated with explicit preconditions, invariants, guard conditions, and postconditions governing admissibility, execution safety, and emergency handling. These requirements support runtime verification and future reactive synthesis approaches. We present an initial lab-based validation demonstrating that voice and GUI-based inputs can be reliably interpreted and safely executed as constrained maneuver requests.

AI.tldr: A requirements-governed maneuver-response model that mediates multi-modal human intent (speech, gestures, GUI) into safe UAV maneuvers by treating operator inputs as bounded maneuver requests rather than direct commands, with formal specification supporting runtime verification.
AI.motivation: Direct human interaction with autonomous UAVs via speech, gestures, and graphical interfaces introduces safety risks as operator requests can conflict with terrain constraints, inter-UAV separation requirements, and flight-envelope limitations.
AI.method: A requirements-governed maneuver-response model where operator inputs are treated as bounded maneuver requests mapped to constrained motion primitives through a structured request-evaluate-execute pipeline. Each request is interpreted with confidence, validated against terrain, separation, workspace, and flight-envelope constraints, and can be constrained, rejected, or executed with continuous runtime monitoring. The approach is formalized as a requirements-based specification model with explicit preconditions, invariants, guard conditions, and postconditions governing admissibility, execution safety, and emergency handling.
AI.result: Initial lab-based validation demonstrates that voice and GUI-based inputs can be reliably interpreted and safely executed as constrained maneuver requests.
AI.conclusion: The requirements-based specification model provides a formal framework for safe human-UAV interaction through multi-modal inputs, supporting runtime verification and future reactive synthesis approaches.

title: Trajectory Planning and Certification for 3-DOF Robot Manipulators Using Real Quantifier Elimination Based on Comprehensive Gröbner Systems
summary: We propose an algorithm and its implementation for trajectory planning and certification for 3-DOF robot manipulators. The method uses Real Quantifier Elimination (QE) based on Comprehensive Gröbner Systems (CGS), also known as the CGS-QE method. The main advantage of the proposed method is its efficiency in trajectory planning and solution certification. This efficiency comes from the effective use of the CGS. First, for trajectory planning, we solve the inverse kinematics problem at each point along the trajectory via Gröbner basis computation. This usually requires recalculating the Gröbner basis at every point, which is time-consuming. We avoid this by computing the CGS for a parametric system. Here, the end-effector coordinates are parameters. This approach streamlines the algorithm. Second, for solution certification, the CGS-QE method certifies that an inverse kinematics solution exists at any point along the end-effector's trajectory. Our method also certifies solutions for trajectories composed of line segments and cubic natural splines. The algorithm is implemented within the computer algebra system Risa/Asir.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CGS-QE (Comprehensive Gröbner Systems-based Real Quantifier Elimination) algorithm and implementation for efficient trajectory planning and solution certification of 3-DOF robot manipulators.
AI.motivation: The authors address the computational inefficiency of recalculating Gröbner bases at each point during trajectory planning and the need for rigorous solution certification in robot manipulator control.
AI.method: The method uses Real Quantifier Elimination based on Comprehensive Gröbner Systems (CGS). It treats end-effector coordinates as parameters in a parametric system, avoiding repeated Gröbner basis computations. The approach handles trajectories composed of line segments and cubic natural splines, implemented in Risa/Asir.
AI.result: The CGS-QE method achieves significant efficiency gains in trajectory planning and provides rigorous solution certification for inverse kinematics problems along arbitrary trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm effectively streamlines 3-DOF robot manipulator trajectory planning and solution verification, demonstrating the practical utility of CGS-based approaches in robotics applications.

title: Self-Healing Visual Recovery for Autonomous Ground Vehicles Using Camera-Only Visual Odometry
summary: Low-cost unmanned ground vehicles are often used in indoor places like warehouses, inspection corridors, and farm rows, where painted floor lines guide the robot. Line following is useful because it only needs one camera and little computing power, but it can fail when the line is blocked or turns sharply and goes out of view. Sensor-rich platforms tolerate this through hardware redundancy (LiDAR, GPS, multiple cameras), but camera-only systems must recover at runtime with no additional infrastructure. This paper presents a lightweight, two-stage recovery approach that restores guideline tracking without LiDAR, GPS, or a GPU. When the line is lost, the robot first turns in place while slowly relaxing its color checks and waiting for confirmation across multiple frames (Stage 1). If the line is still not found, monocular visual odometry moves the robot back to saved breadcrumb positions before it tries again (Stage 2). The system uses a depth-gated HSV line tracker, a YOLOv8n obstacle detector, and a visual odometry breadcrumb mapper, and it runs at 20 Hz on CPU-only hardware. The controller embeds a complete MAPE-K loop within a single 50 ms control tick, with no external adaptation manager required. The approach is evaluated across 119 fault-injected episodes on three Webots simulation courses. The method was successful in 86.6% of cases, with a median recovery time of 3.26 seconds. These results demonstrate that reliable visual recovery is feasible on camera-only UGVs within practical cost and computational limits.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, two-stage recovery approach for camera-only UGVs that restores guideline tracking without LiDAR, GPS, or GPU by combining in-place color check relaxation with monocular visual odometry breadcrumb navigation.
AI.motivation: Low-cost UGVs in indoor environments use painted floor lines for guidance, but line following can fail when lines are blocked or turns are sharp. Camera-only systems have limited hardware redundancy compared to sensor-rich platforms that can tolerate failures through hardware redundancy (LiDAR, GPS, multiple cameras).
AI.method: Two-stage recovery approach: Stage 1 turns in place while slowly relaxing color checks and waiting for confirmation across multiple frames; Stage 2 uses monocular visual odometry to move robot back to saved breadcrumb positions. System uses depth-gated HSV line tracker, YOLOv8n obstacle detector, and visual odometry breadcrumb mapper. Runs at 20 Hz on CPU-only hardware with a complete MAPE-K loop embedded in a 50 ms control tick.
AI.result: Evaluated across 119 fault-injected episodes on three Webots simulation courses; successful in 86.6% of cases with a median recovery time of 3.26 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Reliable visual recovery is feasible on camera-only UGVs within practical cost and computational limits, demonstrating that camera-only systems can maintain robust operation without expensive hardware redundancy.

title: Automated Synthesis of Facial Mechanisms for Conversational Animatronic Robots
summary: Animatronic faces are a central component of socially interactive robots, enabling rich nonverbal communication through facial articulation. However, state-of-the-art animatronic faces are typically tailored systems: each new facial geometry requires extensive manual mechanical redesign, making large-scale personalization prohibitively slow and costly. In this work, we pursue automated and scalable mechanical face synthesis, aiming to rapidly generate a physically realizable facial mechanism for a wide range of facial geometries. We introduce a parametric, linkage-driven mechanical face template whose topology and actuator layout are explicitly parameterized to support systematic scaling and retargeting across diverse facial morphologies. Building on this template, we propose a hierarchical automatic design algorithm that takes a single 2D portrait as input, reconstructs a target 3D face, and synthesizes a collision-free, manufacturable internal mechanism. The algorithm combines anatomy-guided feasible motion volumes, Action Unit (AU)-derived trajectory-based expressiveness objectives, and a collision-driven outer-loop refinement strategy. Beyond hardware synthesis, we argue that future mechanical faces deployed at scale must engage in bidirectional, multi-turn conversation rather than functioning solely as speaking or listening heads. To this end, we develop a dual-identity conversational facial motion synthesis framework that jointly models speaking and listening behaviors from audio, producing temporally coherent 3D facial motion suitable for physical execution. We validate our system through extensive experiments, including (i) quantitative evaluation of automatic mechanism synthesis across diverse facial geometries, (ii) comparisons against manual mechanical design, (iii) benchmarks on conversational facial motion synthesis and real-time deployment, and (iv) perceptual user studies.

AI.tldr: An automated, scalable system for synthesizing physically realizable animatronic faces from 2D portraits, combining parametric mechanical templates with AI-driven design algorithms and dual-identity conversational motion synthesis.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art animatronic faces are custom-built systems requiring extensive manual redesign for each new facial geometry, making large-scale personalization prohibitively slow and costly.
AI.method: A parametric, linkage-driven mechanical face template with explicitly parameterized topology and actuator layout, combined with a hierarchical automatic design algorithm that reconstructs 3D faces from 2D portraits and synthesizes collision-free, manufacturable internal mechanisms using anatomy-guided motion volumes, AU-derived trajectory objectives, and collision-driven refinement. The system also includes a dual-identity conversational facial motion synthesis framework for joint speaking and listening behaviors.
AI.result: The system successfully synthesizes mechanisms across diverse facial geometries with collision-free designs comparable to manual design. The conversational framework produces temporally coherent 3D motion suitable for real-time deployment, validated through extensive quantitative evaluations, benchmarks, and perceptual user studies.
AI.conclusion: Automated mechanical face synthesis is feasible at scale, enabling efficient personalization of animatronic robots. The dual-identity framework addresses the need for bidirectional conversation capabilities rather than just speaking/listening heads, demonstrating that future mechanical faces must engage in multi-turn conversations.

title: From World Action Models to Embodied Brains: A Roadmap for Open-World Physical Intelligence
summary: Artificial general intelligence ultimately requires agents that can reason and act in the physical world. Action models, vision-language-action policies, and world models have advanced this goal, while World Action Models (WAMs) are particularly promising because they connect candidate interventions with predicted consequences. However, progress remains fragmented: models use incompatible action spaces and prediction targets, datasets and tasks follow different conventions, and runtime systems expose limited interfaces for reuse and evaluation. We review the evolution toward WAMs and organize these limitations into three coupled gaps: model roles and representations, objectives and standardization, and system composition. Building on this analysis, we propose a co-evolution roadmap for physical intelligence centered on the \emph{embodied brain}, a long-term model target for integrating multimodal context, comparing candidate interventions, and issuing state-transition or capability requests rather than direct actuator commands. WAMs provide promising prototypes for its predictive functions, while a physical harness grounds model outputs through tools, controllers, verification, and trace logging. Shared contracts align heterogeneous models, data, tasks, and embodiments, and closed-loop post-training converts verified interaction into reusable experience. Together, these components define a modular physical-intelligence stack for adaptive and self-improving embodied agents.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews progress in World Action Models (WAMs) and proposes a co-evolution roadmap for physical intelligence centered on an "embodied brain" with shared contracts, physical harness, and closed-loop post-training.
AI.motivation: Artificial general intelligence requires agents that can reason and act in the physical world. Current progress in action models, vision-language-action policies, and world models is fragmented due to incompatible action spaces, prediction targets, datasets, tasks, and runtime interfaces.
AI.method: The authors analyze three coupled gaps (model roles/representations, objectives/standardization, system composition) and propose a modular physical-intelligence stack including: embodied brain (long-term model target), WAMs (predictive functions), physical harness (grounding through tools/controllers/verification/trace logging), shared contracts (aligning models/data/tasks/embodiments), and closed-loop post-training (converting verified interaction into reusable experience).
AI.result: The paper presents a comprehensive framework for developing adaptive and self-improving embodied agents through modular system design and co-evolution, with WAMs providing promising prototypes for predictive functions and the physical harness grounding model outputs.
AI.conclusion: The embodied brain concept, combined with WAMs and a physical harness, provides a promising pathway toward robust physical intelligence systems that can integrate multimodal context, compare interventions, and issue state-transition or capability requests rather than direct actuator commands.

title: Requirement-Driven Design of Whole-Body Social Tactile Sensing via Virtual Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Tactile sensing for social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) is designed in a hardware-driven manner, where predefined sensor configurations constrain coverage, spatial resolution, and the range of recognizable gestures. We propose a requirement-driven framework that derives sensing requirements, specifically spatial resolution and placement, directly from interaction data. Using a VR-based platform with haptic feedback, we collected high-resolution whole-body contact distributions across multiple social scenarios, from which we identified nine recurring social touch gestures. Eight gestures were selected for controlled data collection with 18 participants, yielding an open-source dataset of 5,520 trials. Analysis of contact distributions and simulated tactile encodings provides quantitative baselines for skin coverage and sensor density on a humanoid robot platform. While demonstrated on a single robot platform, the methodology is designed to be transferable to other robot morphologies, potentially enabling morphology-specific sensing requirements to be derived prior to hardware fabrication.

AI.tldr: A requirement-driven framework that derives tactile sensing specifications (spatial resolution and placement) from social interaction data, validated with a 5,520-trial dataset of nine social touch gestures, enabling morphology-specific sensor design before hardware fabrication.
AI.motivation: Current tactile sensing in social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) is hardware-driven, constraining coverage, spatial resolution, and gesture recognition capabilities; a data-driven approach is needed to derive optimal sensing requirements.
AI.method: Collected whole-body contact distributions using a VR platform with haptic feedback across social scenarios; selected eight gestures for controlled data collection with 18 participants, generating an open-source dataset of 5,520 trials; analyzed contact distributions and simulated tactile encodings to derive sensing requirements.
AI.result: Identified nine recurring social touch gestures; established quantitative baselines for skin coverage and sensor density on humanoid robots; demonstrated the framework's ability to specify sensing requirements prior to hardware design.
AI.conclusion: The methodology is transferable to other robot morphologies, enabling morphology-specific sensing requirements to be derived before hardware fabrication, potentially improving tactile sensing design in social-physical human-robot interaction.

title: High-level spatial Dubins airplane-based reference smoothing with low-level geometric tracking for quadrotor control
summary: A method for the control of quadrotors is presented. It is composed of a high-level reference smoothing step and a low-level reference tracking step. The high-level step leverages the Dubins airplane model for dimensionality reduction and reduced computational complexity, and exploits its structure for decoupling, spatial modeling and the formulation of a small linear program. The low-level step leverages a geometric tracking controller, which is based on the full quadrotor model. The method is designed for the tracking of references subject to lateral constraints along the path. An example is the tracking of references along obstacle contours. It is differentiated between two different setups. Either the high-level planning step is conducted once and offline, or, alternatively, the high-level planning step is conducted recedingly online in closed-loop over a limited spatial prediction horizon.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quadrotor control method combining high-level reference smoothing using the Dubins airplane model for dimensionality reduction and low-level geometric tracking with the full quadrotor model. It handles lateral constraints like obstacle contour tracking and can be implemented either offline or online with receding horizon planning.
AI.motivation: The research addresses the challenge of controlling quadrotors to track references subject to lateral constraints along paths, such as obstacle contours, requiring efficient control while maintaining computational feasibility.
AI.method: The method comprises two steps: (1) High-level reference smoothing using the Dubins airplane model for dimensionality reduction, decoupling, spatial modeling, and linear program formulation; (2) Low-level geometric tracking controller based on the full quadrotor model. Two implementation modes are offered: offline high-level planning or online receding horizon planning with limited spatial prediction.
AI.result: The approach successfully enables quadrotor tracking of references with lateral constraints (e.g., obstacle contours) by leveraging the Dubins airplane model's structure for computational efficiency while maintaining full model fidelity in the low-level controller.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides an effective solution for quadrotor control with lateral constraints, offering flexibility in implementation (offline vs. online planning) and computational efficiency through dimensionality reduction in the high-level planning step.

title: AutoPath: Learning Transferable Goal-Conditioned Stochastic Path Prior for Safe Navigation Without Human Demonstrations
comment: Accepted by IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Real-time navigation in cluttered and dynamic environments requires collision-free and dynamically feasible motion under limited perception. However, feasible navigation behaviors are inherently multimodal because multiple paths may exist around obstacles. In this paper, we formulate navigation as learning a transferable goal-conditioned stochastic path prior that models a reusable distribution over goal-aligned geometry-consistent local paths conditioned on local observations. This formulation enables structured sampling of navigation candidates, allowing multiple feasible paths to be explored through sampling without relying on robot-specific motion constraints. To this end, we introduce a goal-aligned canonical state representation that removes in-plane rotational ambiguity and normalizes local geometry with respect to the goal, enabling rotation-invariant path distribution learning. We further develop a structured prior learning framework that parameterizes local paths using a geometry-aware polar action manifold and incorporates risk-sensitive utility shaping with multi-goal distributional rollouts for stable and safety-aware planning. Extensive experiments in dense static environments and dynamic pedestrian scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method achieves consistently high success rates with competitive efficiency while enabling cross-platform transfer of a single path prior learned on differential-drive robots to quadruped platforms without retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a goal-conditioned stochastic path prior learning framework for navigation in cluttered/dynamic environments. It uses a geometry-aware polar action manifold and risk-sensitive utility shaping to enable structured sampling of collision-free paths, achieving high success rates and cross-platform transfer from differential-drive robots to quadrupeds without retraining.
AI.motivation: Real-time navigation in cluttered and dynamic environments requires collision-free, dynamically feasible motion under limited perception. Feasible navigation behaviors are inherently multimodal because multiple paths exist around obstacles. Existing methods often rely on robot-specific motion constraints, making them less transferable across platforms.
AI.method: The paper formulates navigation as learning a goal-conditioned stochastic path prior that models a distribution over goal-aligned geometry-consistent local paths conditioned on local observations. Key components include: (1) Goal-aligned canonical state representation to remove rotational ambiguity and normalize local geometry; (2) Geometry-aware polar action manifold for parameterizing local paths; (3) Risk-sensitive utility shaping with multi-goal distributional rollouts for safety-aware planning; (4) Structured sampling of navigation candidates without robot-specific motion constraints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in dense static environments and dynamic pedestrian scenarios demonstrate: (1) Consistently high success rates with competitive efficiency; (2) Cross-platform transfer capability - a single path prior learned on differential-drive robots successfully transfers to quadruped platforms without retraining; (3) The method enables structured exploration of multiple feasible paths through sampling.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully achieves high-performance, transferable navigation in complex environments by learning a reusable path prior distribution. The approach enables safe, collision-free navigation across different robot platforms (differential-drive and quadrupeds) through a single learned model, demonstrating the effectiveness of the geometry-aware canonical representation and structured prior learning framework.

title: A Compact Top-Loading Robot for Endovascular Interventions: Design, Control and Evaluation
summary: Robot-assisted endovascular intervention can potentially reduce radiation exposure, improve surgeon ergonomics, enable telesurgery, support active assistance and autonomy, and enhance procedural precision. However, existing systems often suffer from limited procedural coverage because constrained patient-side setups, restricted flexibility, and complex instrument exchange hinder clinical workflow integration. This work presents a compact robotic system for endovascular interventions that enables continuous translational and rotational manipulation of standard endovascular instruments. The system consists of two alternating carts with pneumatically actuated membrane grippers integrated into rotating gripper gears. Its top-loading design allows rapid exchange of instruments such as guidewires and catheters without changing the robotic setup. A leader-follower control strategy enables continuous motion despite the finite stroke of each cart. The system was evaluated in motion-tracking experiments with guidewires and catheters and in an in vitro vascular phantom. The motion-tracking experiments showed generally smooth translational and rotational motion profiles. Across all tested guidewire and catheter experiments, the mean relative tracking errors were 3.6% for translational motion and 4.1% for rotational motion. In the vascular phantom, robot-assisted navigation reached the target in most trials, demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed manipulation concept under in vitro conditions. The presented robotic system demonstrates technical feasibility for continuous manipulation of standard endovascular instruments in bench-top and in vitro experiments. The compact top-loading design may ease instrument exchange and clinical workflow integration. Future work will focus on improving gripping performance, actuation speed, force feedback, and evaluation in more clinically realistic settings.

AI.tldr: A compact robotic system for endovascular interventions that enables continuous translational and rotational manipulation of standard endovascular instruments via a top-loading design with pneumatically actuated grippers and leader-follower control.
AI.motivation: Existing robot-assisted endovascular systems suffer from limited procedural coverage due to constrained patient-side setups, restricted flexibility, and complex instrument exchange that hinder clinical workflow integration.
AI.method: Two alternating carts with pneumatically actuated membrane grippers integrated into rotating gripper gears. A leader-follower control strategy enables continuous motion despite finite cart stroke. The top-loading design allows rapid instrument exchange (guidewires, catheters) without changing the robotic setup.
AI.result: Motion-tracking experiments showed smooth translational (3.6% mean relative error) and rotational (4.1% mean relative error) motion profiles. In vascular phantom experiments, robot-assisted navigation reached the target in most trials, demonstrating feasibility under in vitro conditions.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates technical feasibility for continuous manipulation of standard endovascular instruments in bench-top and in vitro experiments. The compact top-loading design may ease instrument exchange and clinical workflow integration. Future work will focus on improving gripping performance, actuation speed, force feedback, and clinical evaluation.

title: MIRA: A Modular Open-Source Micro-UAV for Indoor Research
summary: Indoor robotics research increasingly relies on micro-UAVs whose airframe, electronics, and control software are fully open to modification. Off-the-shelf platforms rarely expose the low-level access required for such modifications, while building a custom alternative typically requires substantial engineering effort before flight testing can begin, leaving many laboratories to work within constraints that limit the scope of their research. We present MIRA (Modular Indoor Research Architecture), a low-cost, open-source micro-UAV for indoor research built around a replicable 3D-printed PLA airframe and a containerized low-level software package managing the companion-to-autopilot communication bridge via Micro XRCE-DDS. Designed as a white-box architecture, core subsystems are individually replaceable without firmware refactoring, supporting local fabrication and component substitution from existing lab inventory. We characterize MIRA through manual flight in position-control mode within an optical motion-capture volume, where the communication pipeline sustains a median companion-to-autopilot latency of 0.02 ms and power spectral density analysis confirms the structural vibration energy stays concentrated in a narrow 90 to 110 Hz band, isolated from the sub-20 Hz control bandwidth and within the autopilot safety thresholds.

AI.tldr: MIRA is a low-cost, open-source micro-UAV for indoor research featuring a 3D-printed PLA airframe and containerized software with a companion-to-autopilot bridge via Micro XRCE-DDS, achieving 0.02 ms latency and isolated structural vibrations in the 90-110 Hz band.
AI.motivation: Indoor robotics research requires micro-UAVs with open, modifiable architectures, but off-the-shelf platforms lack low-level access while custom solutions demand excessive engineering effort before flight testing.
AI.method: MIRA (Modular Indoor Research Architecture) employs a 3D-printed PLA airframe, containerized low-level software managing companion-to-autopilot communication via Micro XRCE-DDS, and a white-box architecture with individually replaceable subsystems.
AI.result: Manual position-control flight in an optical motion-capture volume achieved a median companion-to-autopilot latency of 0.02 ms, with structural vibrations concentrated in a narrow 90-110 Hz band isolated from the sub-20 Hz control bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: MIRA provides a viable, low-cost, open-source platform that enables extensive modification without firmware refactoring, overcoming the limitations of both commercial and custom solutions for indoor research applications.

title: Casting Everything to Online API Services? A Survey of Integrating Localized Speech Recognition Models in Robotic Systems
comment: accepted in 18th International Conference on Social Robotics (ICSR + ART 2026)
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has become a critical component of modern robotic systems because it is one of the most natural and intuitive ways for humans to interact with robots. A commonly used method is to directly use API services online. But is that all we can do? This article provides an overview of how ASR technologies are integrated into various intelligent robots and machines. We discuss the evolution of speech recognition from established approaches to state-of-the-art deep learning models, such as OpenAI's Whisper. We also list large-scale datasets and open source toolkits that have been widely used in both industry and academia. We structure the survey around ASR model families, deployment strategies in robotics (especially ROS-based, cloud-based, and hybrid solutions), and several real-world robotic platforms. Finally, we outline the challenges of deploying robust speech recognition in robots and discuss future directions, including multimodal interaction in diverse and dynamic environments. This paper can help social robotics researchers better navigate the emerging domain of language-based natural human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of how Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technologies are integrated into intelligent robots, covering the evolution from traditional methods to state-of-the-art deep learning models, deployment strategies, and real-world robotic platforms.
AI.motivation: To help social robotics researchers navigate the emerging domain of language-based natural human-robot interaction beyond commonly used online API services.
AI.method: Structured survey covering ASR model families, deployment strategies (ROS-based, cloud-based, hybrid solutions), real-world robotic platforms, large-scale datasets, and open source toolkits.
AI.result: Provides overview of ASR technology evolution, state-of-the-art models (e.g., Whisper), deployment strategies, and real-world platforms while identifying challenges and future directions.
AI.conclusion: Outlines challenges of deploying robust speech recognition in robots and discusses future directions including multimodal interaction in diverse and dynamic environments.

title: Robust bipedal locomotion on flowable slopes via foot-driven terrain manipulation
summary: Bipedal robots are challenging to control because they operate close to instability, where small variations in foot-terrain contact can rapidly destabilize locomotion. On rigid terrain, bipedal robots mitigate this fragility by using well-established contact mechanics and control strategies. On flowable surfaces such as granular slopes, foot contact can induce large surface deformations and solid-fluid-like transitions, coupling terrain effects with robot dynamics, leading to underperformance or failure. This is partly due to the lack of reliable methods to represent the dynamics of flowable terrain, making it difficult to account for terrain effects in locomotion design. Here, we investigate how controlling terrain response can improve bipedal locomotion on granular slopes by studying the terradynamics of cleated feet, thin plates emanating from the foot soles. Systematic studies of a small-scale (1.4 kg) robophysical biped reveal that cleats with sparse and dense spacing lead to excessive terrain yielding and resistance, respectively, degrading performance and leading to failure. An intermediate cleat spacing distributes interaction forces to maintain substrate stresses near (or below) the yield threshold, enabling walking on granular slopes up to 30 degrees. Guided by these principles, we design a foot that actively adjusts cleat depth and accommodates both rigid and granular terrain. We also demonstrate that the principles of effective foot-terrain interaction translate to a larger (15 kg) autonomous biped. Our study presents an alternative to conventional body-centric robot control approaches, which regulate terrain-induced effects through body motion, by instead regulating terrain interactions through limb-centric approach.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how controlling foot-terrain interaction through cleated foot design and active depth adjustment can improve bipedal robot locomotion on granular slopes, presenting a limb-centric alternative to conventional body-centric control approaches.
AI.motivation: Bipedal robots face significant control challenges on flowable surfaces like granular slopes due to large foot-terrain deformations and solid-fluid-like transitions that couple terrain effects with robot dynamics. The lack of reliable methods to represent flowable terrain dynamics makes it difficult to account for terrain effects in locomotion design, leading to underperformance or failure.
AI.method: Systematic studies were conducted on a small-scale (1.4 kg) robophysical biped to investigate terradynamics of cleated feet. Cleat spacing was varied to study effects on walking performance on granular slopes. Based on findings, a foot with active cleat depth adjustment was designed and tested on both rigid and granular terrain. The principles were then demonstrated on a larger (15 kg) autonomous biped.
AI.result: Cleats with sparse spacing cause excessive terrain yielding and resistance, degrading performance. Cleats with dense spacing also degrade performance due to excessive resistance. Intermediate cleat spacing distributes interaction forces to maintain substrate stresses near (or below) the yield threshold, enabling walking on granular slopes up to 30 degrees. The active foot design successfully translates these principles to a larger biped.
AI.conclusion: This study presents an alternative to conventional body-centric robot control approaches (which regulate terrain-induced effects through body motion) by instead regulating terrain interactions through a limb-centric approach, enabling effective bipedal locomotion on challenging flowable terrains.

title: A Minimalist Retargeting-Guided Reinforcement Learning Recipe for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Recent work in humanoid whole-body control has found success with a simple recipe: retarget human motion to robot kinematic references, then train policies via reinforcement learning (RL) to track them. But how does this recipe transfer to dexterous manipulation? The answer is not obvious, as manipulation involves complex, contact-rich dynamics and requires delicate regulation of contact modes and forces. We present REGRIND, a minimalist retargeting-guided RL pipeline that learns dexterous manipulation policies from a single human demonstration. REGRIND retargets human hand-object motion to a robot reference that preserves hand-object spatial and contact relationships, trains a residual RL policy in simulation to track object-centric keypoints along that reference, and transfers the resulting policy zero-shot to hardware with careful system identification. The resulting policies produce fluid, human-like behavior on two different multi-fingered hands across contact-rich tool-use tasks, including operating a pair of scissors and turning a screwdriver. Through systematic hardware experiments, we identify and analyze the key factors that govern sim-to-real transfer in dexterous manipulation, offering practical guidance for retargeting-based learning in contact-rich settings. Videos and code are available at https://yunhaifeng.com/REGRIND.

AI.tldr: REGRIND is a minimalist retargeting-guided RL pipeline that learns dexterous manipulation policies from a single human demonstration, retargets human hand-object motion to robot reference, trains residual RL policy to track object-centric keypoints, and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer producing fluid human-like behavior on multi-fingered hands for tasks like using scissors and screwdrivers.
AI.motivation: While retargeting + RL has succeeded in humanoid whole-body control, this approach is not obvious for dexterous manipulation due to complex contact-rich dynamics and the need for delicate regulation of contact modes and forces.
AI.method: REGRIND pipeline consists of: (1) retargeting human hand-object motion to robot reference preserving spatial and contact relationships; (2) training a residual RL policy in simulation to track object-centric keypoints along the reference; (3) zero-shot transfer to hardware with careful system identification.
AI.result: Policies produce fluid, human-like behavior on two different multi-fingered hands across contact-rich tool-use tasks, including operating scissors and turning a screwdriver. Systematic hardware experiments identify key factors governing sim-to-real transfer in dexterous manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The work offers practical guidance for retargeting-based learning in contact-rich settings, demonstrating that a simple retargeting-guided RL approach can effectively learn dexterous manipulation from a single human demonstration.

title: Mixture of Frames Policy: Multi-Frame Action Denoising for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation is inherently multi-frame: local actions may be simple in an end-effector frame, while transport, upright-object handling, and whole-body coordination are better represented in a base-aligned frame. However, modern diffusion-based visuomotor policies typically commit to a single predefined action frame, forcing one denoiser to model action distributions that are often unnecessarily complex in that frame. We propose Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF), a diffusion policy that performs synchronized action denoising across multiple coordinate frames. MoF maintains a single canonical diffusion state, re-expresses it in several task-relevant frames, applies frame-specialized denoisers, and fuses their noise predictions back in the canonical frame. To make this possible for intermediate noisy diffusion states, we introduce a column-based 6D rotation representation within an SE(3) action parameterization that supports exact, differentiable frame transformations without requiring noisy rotations to lie on the SO(3) manifold. Across nine simulated bimanual manipulation tasks, we show that the best action frame is task-dependent and that MoF improves over oracle frame selection and standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) baselines. We further evaluate MoF on two real-world bimanual mobile manipulation tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms all constituent single-frame baselines. Project homepage: https://mofpo.github.io

AI.tldr: MoF is a diffusion policy that performs synchronized action denoising across multiple coordinate frames, improving robotic manipulation by using frame-specialized denoisers and fusing their predictions, outperforming single-frame and MoE baselines on both simulated and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation is inherently multi-frame, with different tasks requiring different coordinate frames (e.g., end-effector vs. base-aligned frames). Modern diffusion policies commit to a single predefined frame, forcing one denoiser to model complex action distributions that could be simpler in other frames.
AI.method: MoF maintains a single canonical diffusion state, re-expresses it in several task-relevant frames, applies frame-specialized denoisers, and fuses their noise predictions back in the canonical frame. It introduces a column-based 6D rotation representation within SE(3) for exact, differentiable frame transformations.
AI.result: Across nine simulated bimanual manipulation tasks, MoF shows the best action frame is task-dependent and improves over oracle frame selection and standard MoE baselines. On two real-world bimanual mobile manipulation tasks, MoF outperforms all constituent single-frame baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-frame approaches are essential for robotic manipulation, and MoF effectively handles task-dependent action frames while achieving state-of-the-art performance on both simulated and real-world tasks.
